THE LATE RIGHT HONOURABLE JULES LEGER
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said yesterday, with the death of Jules Leger, Canada is losing one of its most prominent sons and servants.

All Canadians were filled with admiration for the strength of his spirit, the wisdom and dignity with which he performed the duties of the high office of Governor General in spite of the stroke which he suffered early during his mandate. [Translation]
Madam Speaker, we often admire in others and especially in great men, the qualities that we would like to have ourselves. That is why every one of us will admire such and such aspect of the character and life of the former Governor General. As far as I am concerned, it is the quality, the extent and catholicity of his patriotism which were paramount in Jules Leger, as well as the extreme generosity with which he served the public good. He also had a sense of history and a concern for lucid expression, which might explain why he was at first attracted by journalism. I also appreciated his kindness and the obvious relish with which he underlined the humorous aspects of life.

He has given us many standards to emulate. One of them was the harmony of his married life. His wife, Gabrielle, shared in his duties, burdens and accomplishments. In this she served all Canadians. Today all Canadians share in her sorrow.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: THE LATE RIGHT HONOURABLE JULES LEGER
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, on behalf of the Official Opposition 1 want to associate ourselves with the words of tribute and deep regret expressed on behalf of the government by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) on the death of His Excellency, former Governor General Leger.
Governor General Leger was an outstanding Canadian who served his country as newspaper editor, as a public servant, as a diplomat of distinction and finally as Governor General. As a member of a distinguished family of Quebec, Jules Leger never lost sight of his rural roots in that province, he never lost the strength of his faith and he never avoided what he knew to
be the responsibilities of his citizenship. Throughout all these years of service Jules Leger had the undaunting support and encouragement of his wife Gabrielle. We shall all remember Mrs. Leger in our prayers today.

Mr. Leger rendered immense services to this country and he deserved the admiration of every Canadian. During his entire career in the public service, he showed great competence and much wisdom. After he was appointed Governor General of Canada, millions of Canadians discovered a man with unequalled courage and determination. Mr. Leger was a great Canadian.

Jules Leger shall always be remembered for his steady, quiet pursuit of excellence. Every task he performed-and he performed several under the most difficult of circumstances-was approached with determination and a clear understanding of what it was he wished to achieve. His vision of Canada as a home for both French and English, where both languages and all cultures could flourish, was a consistent theme in all of his endeavours, whether as ambassador to France in difficult times, or as under-secretary of state during a period of growing cultural and political awareness in his home province of Quebec.
As Governor General, Jules Leger sought to make his office a positive instrument of Canadian identity and to establish Canadian traditions befitting a sovereign nation. We were all saddened by his illness which, so early in his term of office, might have caused a less determined person to stand down. Not Jules Leger. He demonstrated to all Canadians that illness should not deter us from responsibility. We shall always remember his eloquent words in his 1975 New Year's messages when he stated:
These long months have brought me close to those who suffer... They should not despair.
Madam Speaker, we mourn the loss today of Jules Leger, but we do not despair. For the life of Jules Leger is a shining example of public service, of quiet excellence and of the best of the Canadian spirit.
[ Translation]

subsubtopic: ITALIAN EARTHQUAKE-ASSISTANCE BY CANADA-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, under Standing Order 43, I move a motion of urgent and pressing necessity. In view of the devastating earthquake which has struck the Naples-Salerno area of southern Italy, in view of the death toll of over 400 people and the extensive damage to property, and given that Canada has always acted with generosity and swiftness in meeting such natural disasters, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Nepean-Carle-ton (Mr. Baker):
That this House urges the Secretary of State for External Affairs to consult urgently with the Italian government as to the special and immediate needs of the victims of the earthquake of the Naples-Salerno area of southern Italy and that the minister report to the House at the earliest opportunity and advise the House on the ways in which the Canadian government is willing and able to render assistance. Further, that the government consult with the many Canadians who wish personally to assist the victims of this earthquake and provide special programs which will allow for the people of Canada with special ties to Italy to respond in an urgent and generous manner through airlifts, emergency relief and reconstruction.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF SERVICES OF WEST COAST WEATHERSHIPS- -MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 1 rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 to present a motion which is of urgent importance and pressing necessity. Given that the federal government has unwisely decided to terminate the services of the two Pacific coast weatherships, in spite of the fact that these vessels have provided an essential early warning weather service and scientific data base for several decades, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. McKinnon):
That the government be required to continue the services of the west coast weatherships in accordance with the advice of eminent Canadian scientists, the World Meteorological Association, the United Nations Intergovernmental Oceanographic Commission, and the International Council of Scientific Unions, all of whom agree that sea-based reference stations are an essential element of any weather reporting network because they provide necessary data which cannot be measured by an orbiting satellite.

subsubtopic: CONGRATULATIONS ON ESTABLISHMENT OF DAY CARE CENTRE-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a non-partisan matter, which I am sure will receive unanimous consent. As a result of a question I raised last year on the International Day of the Child, which was supported by the then Conservative minister of national health and welfare and members of all parties, a group of women workers have been quietly and persistently working to organize the first day care centre on Parliament Hill. Recently we learned that you, Madam Speaker, have approved use of space in the East Block for a day care centre which will give House of Commons employees adequate care for their children.
In view of the unprecedented action to provide day care in the work place, which is a model that all federal departments should follow, I move, seconded by the hon. member for York South-Weston (Mrs. Appolloni) and the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay):
That this House congratulate Madam Speaker and the House of Commons day care committee for their tireless efforts to establish day care on the Hill.

subsubtopic: CALL FOR TABLING OF NEW BUDGET-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. The federal budget has done and will do nothing to curb inflation. Social programs which are bound by fixed yearly budgets from funding agencies will have to compensate for as much as a 10 per cent to 12 per cent increase in the cost of their operations due to inflation, increases which curtail and limit the effectiveness and service these programs and institutions can provide. Whereas these programs are aimed particularly at native people, low income families, senior citizens, the handicapped and the needy, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Wright):
That this government abandon its misguided budget immediately and table not later than January 15, 1981, a budget which realistically addresses Canada's primary economic enemy, namely inflation.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY RESPECTING URBAN TRANSIT ASSISTANCE TO ONTARIO
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Transport. Will the minister indicate what urban transit assistance will be extended to Ontario this year or next, especially with regard to the metropolitan Toronto area where there is such an increasing transit problem which cannot be solved without federal attention?

subsubtopic: INQUIRY RESPECTING URBAN TRANSIT ASSISTANCE TO ONTARIO
speechtext: Madam Speaker, under the UTAP program, the Urban Transit Assistance Program, each province is entitled to an allocation, relative to the size of its population, of $10 per head. Ontario receives the same treatment as every other province. If my memory serves me well, it amounts to some $86 million a year. Ontario is making full use of that, mostly for grade separation rather than urban transportation in the strict sense of the word.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY RESPECTING URBAN TRANSIT ASSISTANCE TO ONTARIO
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the Minister of Transport must know that the $86 million he is referring to is simply for the type of activity he has mentioned, grade separations on overpasses. Does the minister's answer mean that they intend to renege on commitments made by the federal government to the government of Ontario, namely the Clark government commitment to give up to $10 million per year to assist in transit matters in Ontario; second, the promise made in the 1974 campaign by the Liberal government to give up to $290 million to various provinces; and, finally, the commitment that was made to assist with regard to the realignment of trackage west of the Union station and to redesign the Union station itself. Is the government going to renege on all those commitments?

subsubtopic: INQUIRY RESPECTING URBAN TRANSIT ASSISTANCE TO ONTARIO
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the provinces have extraordinary freedom under the UTAP program. They can use the money for grade separations, or anything related to urban transportation. Some provinces use the money to purchase buses. In certain circumstances, others have even used it to build sidewalks. Therefore, the freedom of the provinces is great. The province of Ontario has decided to use this federal money which has been allocated to them for grade separations only. That is their decision to make.
The hon. member made reference to a commitment of a previous administration to provide $30 million for the Bathurst Union station project. Obviously I have looked at the file. The file answers a request from Mr. Snow for $30 million of UTAP money for that purpose. My distinguished predecessor answered yes to that. A communique issued on the eve of the election leaves it open as to what was offered, but my interpretation is that it was UTAP money that was offered. If there was a commitment to give $30 million extra UTAP money to

Ontario for this subject, it must have been the result of a shaking of hands between my predecessor and Mr. Snow, because there is no reference to it in the file. That is the truth of the matter.

subtopic: INQUIRY WHETHER COMMITMENT TO ONTARIO WILL BE HONOURED
INQUIRY WHETHER COMMITMENT TO ONTARIO WILL BE HONOURED
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to pursue that matter with the Minister of Transport. Before we get too far off the track on this, I might remind the minister that when the government gave Ontario its freedom to spend money on urban transit out of the grade separation program, at the same time it reduced Ontario's grade separation money, thereby putting Ontario in the position where it had to choose between spending less money to save children or helping transit.
Would the minister please advise this House very clearly- because he has not yet done so-whether he proposes to honour the commitment to give Ontario an additional $30 million to help it do something about transit for the first time, or whether in fact he proposes to continue not only the reduction in grade separation programs but also to cancel the $30 million to Ontario, thereby making sure it never gets a penny out of this government for urban transit?

subtopic: INQUIRY WHETHER COMMITMENT TO ONTARIO WILL BE HONOURED
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I will repeat what I have already said. The program is one which allows the provinces to decide in which way they are going to spend their UTAP money. They can spend it on railway grade separation, overpasses and so forth. They can

Oral Questions
spend it on buying buses or for other worthwhile urban transportation objectives.
This is one of the difficulties of the federal system, if I may say so in a reflective mood. If a province decides to use a federal program in a certain way, all the other provinces are bound to ask for similar use of the same program even if they are given the full freedom to use the money in a different fashion. This is a way of adjusting regionalism in this country. It is not always easy, as illustrated by the present series of questions.

subtopic: INQUIRY WHETHER COMMITMENT TO ONTARIO WILL BE HONOURED
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, since we have received a reflective answer, I will ask a question which might draw another. Because this matter is critical. I should point out that this is the first time in the history of any government that a promise on urban transit has been broken twice.
Will the minister explain to me, to Toronto and to Canadians why it is justified to reduce the amount of money for grade separation, to produce no money for urban transit support and to produce a budget which will reduce social spending, all of which means that municipalities must bear an ever greater burden using the less progressive tax system which they have to use? Can the minister justify this in the context of a budget which goes to $80 billion in spending which spends $50 million on more advertising to tell us how good we should feel and which spends less on matters which will help solve the problems we already face?

subtopic: INQUIRY WHETHER COMMITMENT TO ONTARIO WILL BE HONOURED
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as I said in the interview which is referred to at this time, there is no doubt that way back in 1977, or even earlier than that, there was a certain overenthusiasm on the part of the government of the time about the belief that it could spend great amounts of money on urban transportation.
There is no doubt that there is a great need. At the moment, for example, the trend is toward relocation of railway lines. There was a time in the ninetheenth century when it was a status symbol to have a railway line right in the centre of town. The mood of the people has changed; they would like to see it way out of town now. All this is to say that the amount of money which can be allocated to urban transportation is really not unlimited. I will do my very best to increase this amount, knowing full well that it will not go a third of the way to what might be useful.

subtopic: INQUIRY WHETHER COMMITMENT TO ONTARIO WILL BE HONOURED
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is difficult to increase what you have never spent on urban transit. The point is that in 1977 the government took Ontario's share of grade separation funds down from $18 million a year to $16.5 million, and the government said Ontario could spend some of that on urban transit. The effect of this government action is either no funds for urban transit or fewer dollars to help at railway crossings where children are killed.
Can I now have an assurance that, contrary to what some of us believe, the grade separation fund will not be further reduced but will in fact be increased and will be used for its primary and proper purpose, that of saving lives?
November 24, 1980

subtopic: INQUIRY WHETHER COMMITMENT TO ONTARIO WILL BE HONOURED
speechtext: Madam Speaker, that is exactly what I am trying to say. There are different views as to what is needed under the label of urban transportation. Some people say that this is essentially railway separation or overpasses. Ontario believes that. There is less of a need for that in Prince Edward Island, for example. There are fewer railway crossings there, so Prince Edward Island is using the money for other purposes such as buying buses and building some types of sidewalks occasionally. The program was aimed at allowing maximum flexibility to the provinces for what they considered to be important in urban transportation. Previous to that I am the first to admit that Ontario was getting more for railway crossings; but what Ontario considered then to be fair, that is, having 58 per cent of the money under this program, was considered by other provinces not to be fair, so the federal government at the time decided to give for each province an equal amount depending on its population. Some people will consider that fair, others will not.

subsubtopic: OWNERSHIP OF TECHNOLOGY DEVELOPED IN CANADA- GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. On Friday I made public copies of certain correspondence between the Exxon Corporation in the United States and its subsidiary here, Imperial Oil. I understand that the minister himself has copies of that correspondence. In it it is made clear that technology and other patentable information that is developed in Canada by Imperial Oil will reside in its final ownership form with Exxon in the United States. Considering that over the weekend, an official from Imperial Oil confirmed the existence of this arrangement, I would like to ask the minister what steps the government plans to take to reverse this totally unacceptable situation in which Canadian taxpayers are financing a project which ultimately ends up in the United States.

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: OWNERSHIP OF TECHNOLOGY DEVELOPED IN CANADA- GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I contacted the president of Imperial Oil this morning to discuss with him the point the hon. member raised last Friday in order to obtain whatever information is available at this time. I am advised that Imperial Oil modified the policy somewhat in 1979 and that the patents are now issued in Ottawa in the name of Imperial Oil of Canada. However, the arrangement for the pooling of the research remains integrated under Exxon and, obviously, this is a source of concern for Canada not only in the oil and gas industry but also with regard to research and development generally for all firms in this country.
In a review of industrial policy the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce is examining very carefully this whole question of research and development and the assurance that Canadians will first benefit from research and development
November 24, 1980

undertaken in Canada. I have this preliminary information. We, as a government, have stated that we believe there is not enough research and development undertaken by the oil and gas industry inside Canada. We have stated that quite clearly in our energy program and I have done so in several speeches I have made. That is one of the reasons for our program of increasing Canadian ownership to over 50 per cent and ensuring that a significant number of the large oil and gas firms will be Canadian controlled. These are steps which are in the direction of ensuring that we will have large firms in Canada which will conduct research and development in this country.

subsubtopic: OWNERSHIP OF TECHNOLOGY DEVELOPED IN CANADA- GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I will have something to say about the minister's latter point later today when the debate on that important topic resumes. I noticed the minister said that Imperial Oil somewhat modified its policy as of 1979. Since my information is that the Prime Minister was made aware of the policy of Imperial Oil in May, 1976, could he tell us what the government has done in the four-year interval to reverse this totally unacceptable policy? Could he tell us if it is just Imperial Oil which practises this kind of arrangement with its subsidiary, or are Shell, Gulf, Texaco and all other multinationals carrying on the same kind of process?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: OWNERSHIP OF TECHNOLOGY DEVELOPED IN CANADA- GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as far as the first question is concerned, obviously I am not in a position to answer whether or not the Prime Minister received a particular representation. The only thing I have seen is an unsigned letter, and I am not in a position to know whether it was ever received by the Prime Minister.
As to the second point, it appears that it was an anonymous letter which was sent. I checked at a meeting last week with Suncor as to what was happening with the technology which had been developed. For instance, if one takes the case of Suncor, I was assured that the technology and the patents belong to Suncor of Canada and they are here in this country. But one must realize that if a company is 100 per cent foreign owned, even if the patents are held by the Canadian subsidiary in Canada, the patent will belong to the foreign multinational which controls it 100 per cent. This is why our policy of Canadianization of the oil and gas industry becomes so very important, and 1 hope we will get the support of hon. members opposite for this policy in the next few months and years to come.

subsubtopic: OWNERSHIP OF TECHNOLOGY DEVELOPED IN CANADA- GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my party has been calling for that policy for more than 20 years, so we do not need to take any lessons from the Liberals.

subsubtopic: OWNERSHIP OF TECHNOLOGY DEVELOPED IN CANADA- GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

between the minister and a representative of the Imperial Oil company, I should like to ask the minister for two assurances this afternoon: first, that not one additional penny will be granted to Shell; and second, since we have Petro-Canada and the minister is so proud of Petro-Canada, will he finally tell Imperial Oil and Shell that we do not need them in the north, that Petro-Canada can do that development for us?

subsubtopic: OWNERSHIP OF TECHNOLOGY DEVELOPED IN CANADA- GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: OWNERSHIP OF TECHNOLOGY DEVELOPED IN CANADA- GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I am advised that the Shell group, the Alsands group, does not require any financial loans or arrangements; they are not asking for this. They have asked to meet with me again. I met with them a few weeks ago. Certainly I will be available to talk with them further and advise the hon. member as to the results of those talks.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. No doubt at this point he is aware that very many small Canadian oil exploration companies are leaving our country, for the United States particularly but for other parts of the world as well with more hospitable political climates. Many of these companies have already left and have taken with them Canadian expertise, technology and equipment. Since the minister appears to have discovered a mysterious fountain of wealth from which he is drawing $40 million to secure Imperial Oil's confidence in Canada's energy future, what measures does he have in mind to convince Canadian entrepreneurs that, instead of their assets being confiscated, they will be allowed to operate in their own country under fair and equitable rules in comparison to those by which the game is played in other parts of the world?
Try Norway or Mexico.
You try it, Ian.

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the hon. member's question was rather long and convoluted. I should like to remind him that indeed such a policy was put forward in the national energy program. It is totally oriented toward giving advantages to Canadian-owned and controlled companies.
That is why they are all leaving.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Once those companies have examined the program and the implications of the budget, they will realize-

and more and more of them are realizing it at the present time- that indeed the program will be extremely beneficial to them. I can tell the hon. member that we have had discussions with a large number of Canadian-owned companies that consider the program put forward very much to their advantage.
Name them.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: There is no question about confiscating anything. It is a matter of helping Canadian firms grow and enlarging the Canadian control of that particular industry over the next few years.

Madam Speaker, despite what the minister said and his assertion that all is well, the fact remains that there is a mass exodus from western Canada not of multinationals but of Canadian companies to other parts of the world, the effects of which are not only disastrous to our energy future but to the economy in general, particularly in the producing areas of our country where small companies and businesses which service the oil patch are going bankrupt at unprecedented rates. Has the government given any thought to helping these areas most directly affected by the recent budget to overcome this incredibly stupid experiment in energy politics?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader

Fifty per cent.

Madam Speaker, I have a question which I would like to address to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce about the Foreign Investment Review Agency. Generally speaking, in order to obtain approval from the Foreign Investment Review Agency, any person or company wanting to locate or to purchase in Canada must prove that there will be a significant benefit to Canada from the sale or location of the business. How could that be applied in the cases which are simply "deemed approved", given that all that is required is that the agency has not dealt with the application for 60 days in order to achieve "deemed approved" status?
November 24, 1980

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the concept of deeming is simply an alternative to formal order in council approval. When cases are deemed, there is still the assessment by the agency and the negotiation of undertakings, along with consultation with other government departments and provincial governments. So deeming does not mean that there is not the seeking and obtaining of significant benefit to Canada. It is obtained there, just as it is in the case of order in council approval.

In the proposal put forward by Midland Pipe (Canada) Corporation of Calgary in which they were given approval deemed to have been dealt with by the agency to locate a warehouse to import, to gather and to distribute steel oilfield tubing and casing, can the minister explain to the House how the decision was arrived at that they should be allowed to locate this particular operation in Canada, given that there are already at the moment in Canada a large number of companies manufacturing those exact products in western and eastern Canada which are not operating to full capacity? They could use the work and create employment in Canada and they are obviously going to suffer as a result of action by the Foreign Investment Review Agency.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the existing confidentiality requirements of the law, which I hope to have changed over time, prevents me from giving-
Oh, oh!

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans. A few days ago the minister of fisheries announced the implementation of an export licensing system whereby the federal Department of Fisheries would use its definition of product quality as a basis for approving or denying any request to export a quantity of fish to a foreign purchaser. Does the minister have any evidence at all to suggest that Canadian fishing companies are exporting substandard fish products to foreign markets? If so, will the minister name those companies so that all members of the Fisheries Council of Canada may know who these unscrupulous operators are?

speakeroldname: Hon. Romeo LeBlanc (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, there is a problem of consistency of quality and it is in trying to deal with this problem that we are looking at the possibility of grading products before they are exported so importers would know if they are dealing with an A or B quality product. That is not unusual in this type of industry. In
Oral Questions
fact, the industry itself has been requesting that we put more stringent measures on the end product and that we put forward a grading system.

Madam Speaker, my information, obtained from the members of the Fisheries Council, does not concur with the minister's answer. Perhaps he ought to add the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation to his list of shyster companies, in view of their recent multi-million dollar sale of wormy Lake Winnipeg whitefish to Poland in exchange for granting Polish trawlers a quota of Atlantic squid, which Canadian fishermen were not allowed to catch. Be that as it may, why is the minister imposing another bureaucratic burden upon Canadian fishing companies? Will he indicate if export licensing is only the first stage of an orderly marketing philosophy of his which will ultimately lead to a federal monopoly in the marketing of saltwater fish, patterned along the communistic lines of the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation?

Madam Speaker, some of the hon. member's assertions boggle the mind. 1 am not sure if they boggle his mind, but they certainly boggle mine. He starts his question with a gratuitous insult to a Crown corporation which is seen by the fishermen of the freshwater area as having served them well.
Hear, hear!

In fact, it is a corporation which is seen by the provincial premiers and provincial governments as beneficial. It was asked for by them a few years ago, during my predecessor's term of office, and they have not asked that it be abolished or changed radically even when I offered them the opportunity to do so. We are trying to make Canadian fish the highest quality fish exported in the world. I hope hon. members in this House will join with me in this crusade.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, in view of the absence of the Prime Minister, who is still somewhere or other, and the Deputy Prime Minister, I will ask a question of the Acting Prime Minister. November 24, 1980

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (St. John's West):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my supplementary question is for the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, not to the thirty-sixth acting Prime Minister. Enough of this nonsense and gobbledygook when the province of Newfoundland has only 53 per cent of the average earned income of Canadians as a whole. The Newfoundland government has just tabled in connection with their new legislation a report that shows that Hydro-Quebec has benefited by $2 billion since 1972 under the Upper Churchill power contract while the government and people of Newfoundland have benefited by an amount slightly in excess of $100 million net.
In view of the figures I used in my original question, will the minister give the people of Newfoundland a guarantee that he will take steps immediately, first, to use his powers to ensure that Newfoundland can develop the Lower Churchill project and transmit electricity across the province of Quebec, particularly the powers under section 92(10) of the BNA Act; and second, will the minister use his powers to assist the province of Newfoundland in righting this imbalance of income of $2 billion as compared to $100 million, from the Upper Churchill project, a contract which was instituted by a fellow Liberal, Mr. Smallwood, in his heyday in Newfoundland?

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, on the first part of the question I am very happy to tell my friend that not only do I stand ready to correct this situation, or to give the assurance with regard to the transportation of electricity, but the Prime Minister himself is on record as saying, in a letter he wrote to Premier Peckford in October:
In my letter of July 29, 1980, to you I indicated that the federal government stood ready to act if it could clearly be demonstrated that the exportation of electricity from Newfoundland was in fact being prevented by Quebec. This, as you will recall, was also the essence of my comments to you when we discussed the matter at the recent Conference of First Ministers on the Constitution.
So we are on the record in that respect. Madam Speaker.
As far as the second point of the question is concerned, I want to stress to the hon. member that what we are facing is a contract between Quebec-Hydro and, I believe, Rio Tinto, a private British corporation at the time. two parties concerned are willing to have us sit at the table with them.

speechtext:

In view of the fact that some 6,000 to 7,000 jobs are involved in this vital sector of the Canadian manufacturing economy, will the minister respond favourably to the request made to the federal government by Bell Canada and by the government of Ontario that only equipment from those countries which allow Canadian equipment to be attached to their lines should be allowed to be attached to Canadian lines?
[ Translation]

speakeroldname: Hon. Francis Fox (Secretary of State and Minister of Communications):
speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Communications
subsubtopic: ATTACHMENT OF IMPORTED TELEPHONE EQUIPMENT TO CANADIAN LINES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I thank the hon. member for his question, which clearly is very important to the communications industry. As he indicated, the CRTC issued a decision on August 5. Since then a number of applications have been received from provincial governments-the hon. member referred to the Ontario government-and the private sector, on the one hand, to put the CRTC's decision aside, and in other cases to uphold that decision. A number of companies now manufacture in Canada telephones that meet the standards of the FCC in the United States among others and they support the decision. I would also like to point out that, since the initial decision by the CRTC, there has been a significant reduction to the consumer in the price of telephones. But, in any case, we are now reviewing all the questions arising from the petitions before us. My officials have had important discussions with those in the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, to look at the possible implications, and I hope to be in a position to come up with a proposal for a possible solution to those appeals before my cabinet colleagues within a week or two.

Madam Speaker, my supplementary question is for the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. In view of the fact that the vast majority of the cheapest telephones being attached to Canadian phone lines come from Japan, a country with a state-owned national telephone system which does not allow
November 24, 1980

Canadian telephone equipment to be attached to its lines, what action does the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce propose to take to ensure that the jobs of 6,000 to 7,000 Canadians involved in this sector of our manufacturing industry are not threatened by the government's decision?

Since this conference is stressing human rights, economic co-operation, detente in Europe and disarmament, would the hon. minister please indicate to this House why the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, a Crown corporation, did not have at least one reporter attending this conference; and will he assure Canadians that the remainder of the conference, which will continue to sit until March 31, will get better coverage by CBC than it has during the first two weeks of its deliberations?

speakeroldname: Hon. Francis Fox (Secretary of State and Minister of Communications):
speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Communications
subsubtopic: LACK OF COVERAGE OF EUROPEAN CONFERENCE

Madam Speaker, the hon. member is quite right in stressing the importance of the conference that is going on in Madrid. As the hon. member had the courtesy to give me notice of this question just before entering the House this afternoon, I have had the opportunity of checking back with the CBC. speakeroldname: Hon. Mark MacGuigan (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Canada regularly reviews countries' eligibility for Canadian bilateral assistance. Eligibility is determined by a number of factors, among them the major are-developmental need, political and commercial implications, etc. To date, Somalia has not been deemed eligible for Canadian bilateral assistance, although Mission Administered Funds ($25,000 annually) and Canadian Bilateral Food Aid ($3.0 million- 1980/81, $5.0 million in 1974/75 and 1976/77) have been provided. During next year's review of aid eligibility, the Somalian case will be reconsidered.
(a)	No, not at present, although Canada is constantly investigating the situation to determine if further involvement is warranted and can be accommodated within budgetary constraints.
(b)	Canadian NGO's are involved in relief work without assistance from CIDA. CIDA does assist, however, in NGO's rehabilitation efforts (including all second line operations, e.g. logistics support, health care, water, etc.)-in support of humanitarian relief activities. The Canadian Government responds to requests for funds from NGO's and has no specific policy which encourages the NGO's to request funds for country-specific needs. In September-October 1980, however, a group of Canadian NGO representatives participated in a one and a half week mission to Somalia to gain a better understanding of the current situation and how they might best assist in Somalia. Involved in this mission were the CCIC (Canadian Council for International Co-operation), the Overseas Book Centre, the YMCA, and L'AMI (L'assistance medicate internationale). CIDA supported this mission by providing matching funds and by providing briefing assistance to the mission members. CIDA anticipates that NGO projects will be developed in Somalia as a result and that CIDA will be approached for financial assistance to these projects.
(c)	Canada has supported the resolutions of the UN General Assembly concerning the refugee problem in general. It is well recognized by all, including Canada, that the Somalia case is one of the most serious today.

Petroleum Administration Act

The House resumed, from Friday, November 21, consideration of the motion of Mr. Waddell:
That the proclamation laid before the House on Wednesday, November 12, 1980, pursuant to subsection 35(2) of the Petroleum Administration Act, as proclaimed in PC 1980-2915, be revoked.

Mr. Speaker, I am rising today to speak on the Petroleum Administration Act. Following the short comments 1 was able to make on Friday last, 1 wish to underscore again at the beginning that this is a piece of legislation which strikes at the sensitivities of confederation. It will be viewed in western Canada as yet one more attack upon the authority which is granted to us through the British North America Act over the resources of that region.
What we are witnessing at this very moment of our history is a very serious grassroots movement. It has come to the state of vocalization that it has largely on the basis of the constitutional proposals of the federal government, on its energy package, and now because of the decision to establish unilaterally the price of petroleum products. Not only that, but this particular legislation has been brought to the House marinated in the myth that somehow there will be a lack of co-operation among provincial legislatures. What we find is a tremendous lack of will on behalf of the federal government to meet with the producing provinces in a negotiating forum.
Meetings have taken place, but anyone who is following precisely what has been happening knows full well that documentation, one piece after another, from ministers and from the federal government is not in each of those instances a negotiating forum. It is fair to say that by and large, in those meetings that took place during the late summer and fall of this year, the federal government did not negotiate. Yet today we are into this milieu of the federal government pointing to a province, and claiming that in provinces west of Ontario there is ill will in the Canadian family. There is a view that somehow there are partnerships in the family of confederation that are not behaving in the way the federal government wants, and the federal government now wishes to bludgeon them with its own will.
It is imperative upon us all to recognize that we should take a view of what would happen to Canada if the provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan and British Columbia could be given their free opportunity to be able to play their fair and constructive role in confederation. So often it has been portrayed, particularly by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde), that somehow the motives of the western provinces are those of greed. I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that in any careful study of what would happen with greater production in western Canada, there would be an immense benefit to families in central Canada and throughout all of Canada, along with more jobs.

November 24, 1980
Petroleum Administration Act
I ask hon. members to take a look at just one rather remote situation, that of Dome Petroleum, which is presently exploring the north slope of the Arctic. In Dome's estimated spending of $40 billion between 1980 and 1990 to develop five oil fields on our north slope, at least 60 per cent of those dollars, putting together the multiplier effect of some $120 billion, would be spent in central Canada for barge-mounted production facilities, ice breakers and tankers. On this project alone, annual direct and indirect employment would exceed 150,000 man years. It is estimated that the majority of those jobs would be in central Canada.
I say that when the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources tends to perpetuate in his statement, which I view as being false, that somehow there is a position of greed in some part of this region, or that there is a lack of will in some provinces to play the role of good Canadians, he is really exacerbating the situation for his own political gain. I want to underscore that in the developing and producing provinces people are attempting to bring forward proposals by which we would have enhanced development of our petroleum products in Canada. By doing this we would be adding tremendously to the economic and social benefits throughout the whole of Canada.
I want to speak again in direct terms of what happens as we develop each of the tar sands or heavy oil plants. It should be noted that through the 25-year lifetime of a tar sands plant there would be an expenditure of between $60 billion and $65 billion to sustain the investments. There would be another $20 billion for the operation of a particular plant throughout the 25-year period. That gives us a figure of some $85 billion. If we take the Canadian Petroleum Association multiplier effect of 3.4 we find that $290 billion will be pumped into the Canadian system in the next 25 years, over 40 per cent of which would be spent in the province of Ontario. Those numbers should not be jocularly set aside.
Almost half of this $290 billion would be spent, in interesting ways in the province of Ontario. For example, some $800 million would go into iron and steel production. Another $370 million would go into metal fabrication and machinery. Another $325 million would go into transportation equipment. Another $740 million would go into manufacturing and processing. Another $370 million would be for financing from banking institutions, and for trade and services another $750 million. The list goes on.
I find it very perplexing, as one who comes from a part of the country which desires very much to be a member of the Canadian family, to find pressure leaning very heavily upon us to fall into some whip line of doing that which the federal government thinks is right but in fact is counterproductive. In all of this view of Canadianization, and "let the federal government do it," what is the end result?
I phoned the Sweetgrass, Montana, border crossing to ask about the number of Canadian rigs leaving the country. I was told they simply could not keep up with the daily processing of rigs. One man told me they were leaving in droves. Another said that never in his life had he seen so many Canadian oil
rigs leaving this country as he has seen since the last federal budget. On one hand we have the minister, in his sinister way, telling Canadians that he is attempting to Canadianize the oil industry. On the other hand he chases that very industry out of the country.
The situation is even worse than in 1974 when we had 22 taxation policy changes in one fiscal year. At that time they chased 30 per cent of the Canadian-owned oil drilling rigs out of Canada and into other countries.
Let us look at what is happening under this disguise to convince Canadians that the federal government has their interests at heart. The people of central Canada are losing jobs. Manufacturing has to slow down its production. People in all parts of the country have to bear the burden of increased federal debt because the money is not circulating here. We have, instead, a mentality which says that by the middle of this decade $8.5 billion will be taken out of Canada for the purchase of oil from some foreign country for use east of the Ottawa Valley line. By taking these billions of dollars out of Canada and giving them to some foreign country, not a single job will be created in this land. All that you do is make some other nation rich, whether it be Mexico, Venezuela, or the Middle East. While some of those nations may need extended wealth, it is not necessarily the obligation of Canada to provide it. We have the wherewithal, but we need a sense of co-operation from the federal government to put together a petroleum package which will sustain itself and work to the advantage of all Canadians.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is now spending his 40 days and 40 nights in the desert getting $40 a barrel oil. I submit that one tar sands plant would produce more daily oil than he contracted for in Saudi Arabia. Somehow he is over there talking about security of supply. What a nonsensical statement from the leader of this country. With one tar sands plant we would have greater security of supply than by travelling to some foreign land looking for security there. What absolute rubbish, to try to make Canadians think somehow we can have greater security from the Arab nations than from our own provinces. If one would analyse the situation, one would not believe that there is such a shortage in our nation today that we could not have security of supply from within our own borders.
I know that these points I am mentioning are very distressing to western Canadians. The word separation is certainly being used all too often in my part of Canada. When I heard the word being repeated last summer with ever-increasing frequency, I became very much alarmed. I thought there might be a will within my constituency that they could somehow go it alone. If you talked to someone for five minutes, that might be his view. However, if you talked to any of them for an hour, you soon find that it is not Lake of the Woods, Summerside, Shawinigan, old Quebec City or other parts of the country about which they are disgruntled. It is the Prime
November 24, 1980

Minister, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, and this federal government from which they want to separate.
The government is trying to create the myth that there are bad Canadians, and enemies that we have to set other Canadians against. The will of the provinces of Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia has always been to play their role. We live in a milieu of distortion. Because it is in power, the federal government, with its own poisonous thoughts, thinks it can do everything better than the regions.
Let us look at the notion that oil companies will become 50 per cent Canadian owned. Canadians should know that they are not talking about Canadian ownership. There will not be a single Canadian owning one share in a Canadian oil industry if this government has its way. They are talking about government ownership.
We in western Canada have reason to be suspicious when the federal government, not the citizens of Canada, wants a share of an industry which affects only one or two provinces. Is that not reason to suspect it is not in the interests of Canadians but in the interests of protecting the power of the federal government? Should it not raise the eyebrows of people west of the Ontario-Manitoba border when they hear that the oil industry, which is a multinational, ought to be 50 per cent Canadian owned? The federal government did not choose all multinationals, it singled out some of them.
This year Chrysler Corporation is to receive $240 million in guaranteed loans, and a study is being made into Massey-Fer-guson to see whether the federal government can help that multinational corporation. Why is the myth being created that multinationals are good in one region of the country but bad in another region? Surely the criteria must be extended beyond that. There should be a criterion for all multinational corporations in Canada, so that Canadians have the right to buy the shares.
The government must not take the view of singling out multinationals for government control simply to pick on a particular region. Canadians ought to rise up and say that is unfair and unjust. They must take a stand against a government which takes the position that, as the arbitrator operating out of the population basin of the country, it will make and impose decisions upon the regions regardless of their desire to play a part in the fulfilment of Canada's wishes and needs.
In my part of the country, the province of Alberta, there is a strong desire to play a greater part in the building of a better Canada. We can do that by developing upon the strength that is ours. Rather than send billions of dollars out of the country to purchase offshore oil, we should develop our oil here which will create spinoff jobs and great employment opportunities in virtually every region of this land. If we can capitalize on our strengths and build on them, what a great country we would have.
We must be the laughing stock of virtually every nation in the world. In Japan the only resources are fish and tin, yet they have one of the strongest economies in the world. Here we have virtually every resource a country could want. We have

ambitious and educated people. We are lacking only because we have a Liberal government which goes to other countries to purchase, and therefore creates employment there.
This government has failed to commit the people of Canada to the development of what we have here because, for the purpose of re-election, this government would rather create enemies in the family, gather a few of the partners together and point fingers. Once the government has finished pointing fingers it creates a group which says, "In this atmosphere of fear we will rise up and resist those who are branded as enemies". If this attitude continues, the grassroots movement operating today in western Canada without a leader may well find a leader.
This government may seem to be destroying this country with its desire to stay in power, but there is a will in every part of this country to serve this country. Those who display a different attitude and try to persuade Canadians that there is not that will, are simply not speaking the truth. Starting now, I submit that every Canadian should travel more extensively in this country to find out how very much it is the government which is wrong. There are great opportunities for employment in all the regions of Canada. How can we possibly justify a government which destroys those opportunities for work?
Let us discuss just a few of the companies whose positions would be enhanced if we had policies which allowed them to go forward. Canadian Fahramet has four plants in Orillia, Ontario. The company manufactures heat corrosive and abrasive resistent castings used in the petrochemical industry, and equipment for oil rigs. Last month it laid off 33 of its workers. There was a total of 500.
As a direct result of the last budget a Stratford manufacturing firm withdrew a half million dollar contract and rescheduled orders amounting to several million dollars. The company is indifferent as to completion dates.
A drilling company, Simmons Drilling Company of Calgary, purchased $180,000 worth of new cars and trucks last year. Because of the budget ten of its 17 oil rigs have now moved to the United States. The president of Simmons estimates that there is probably a need for three times that number of vehicles this year. Unfortunately, those vehicles will now be purchased in the United States. Let us remember that last year the company purchased $180,000 worth of vehicles in Canada. It now needs three times that number, and because of the budget of this government those vehicles will be purchased in another country.

Mr. Speaker, I want to extend my appreciation to hon. members for their courtesy, even though it is my choice not to extend my remarks but only to conclude.
I say in all sincerity that there is a will amongst the partners in confederation. We believe that resources belong to the provinces. It has worked that way for 113 years for Ontario, Quebec, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia. It has worked that way throughout confederation. The tables have turned and another region now has resources, in this case petrochemical resources. That region is saying to Canadians that they can have that resource at 75 per cent of the Chicago composite price, in spite of the fact that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources talks about selfish people talking about the world price. I say to the minister that that is utter nonsense. That has never been the position of western Canada. There is a 25 per cent advantage over the United States price guaranteed ad infinitum. That is the package from the provinces, yet government members continue to say that there is greed.
Throughout history the west has bought virtually everything at above world prices. Not only do we pay world prices but we also pay discriminatory freight rates. Automobiles, farm machinery and anything manufactured, have been purchased at prices higher than world prices. Today the province of Alberta sells its oil at below the world price. Its contribution to confederation is now in excess of some $20 billion, yet there is the feeling among government members that this should be dismissed and that prices should be cheaper yet.
If hon. members opposite say that the west is making too much money on light and medium weight crude, perhaps there could be some argument. However, the availability of light and medium weight crude will be zero in eight years. At that time we will have a supply of secondary recovery, offshore, north slope, heavy oils and tar sands. The method used to extract each of those is enormously more expensive. We are now receiving $16.75 for oil when it costs us $22 to produce tar sands oil. If there is to be a guarantee of supply, we need an enormous commitment to get plants in place.
Just this year we have lost a $7 billion plant which was ready for construction. The company involved said it could not operate with this government. Just last week another $8 billion plant closed down. The company said that with this government in power it cannot operate. This government is guaranteeing Canadians cheaper oil, when it is very uncertain whether there will be any oil at all. This government is destroying the industry. It is removing incentive and the potential for discovering new methods. 1 could go on about this for quite some time.
We have no energy crisis because we have very ample supplies of petroleum and coal. Each could last hundreds and hundreds of years. We do not have an energy crisis today, but we have a systems crisis brought on not by the greed of westerners for money but very much by the hunger of a Liberal government for power. This is not a question of supply or of dollars. It is a question of power. The federal government is trying to wrench power from the provinces, to the detriment of the fabric of Canada. Canadians should realize that, and if
they do they will understand the views of westerners who say that throughout the course of confederation one set of rules has applied, and now there is a new wealth in their region. Because of this the federal government wants to change the rules of the game, even though in the spirit of co-operation the western provinces have said that they will take only 75 per cent of the Chicago composite price.
I will conclude by saying that we ought not to underestimate the grassroots movement of western Canada. We can have a better Canada if we change disruptive policies. However, if we continue with this Liberal government, I very much fear that we could end up with no Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. E. F. Whelan (Minister of Agriculture):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, first of all I want to make a couple of comments about some of the remarks of the hon. member who spoke before me. I am sure he does not want to leave the impression that it was because of eastern Canada and its industrial base that he said Canadians paid more for farm machinery. Farm machinery has been subjected to no tariff since the 1930s. One can bring in farm machinery from the western United States that was made in the United States. The bulk of it is moved from central Canada to the United States, to the huge assembly plants and fabrication plants in that part of the world. There has been no duty on farm machinery coming into Canada since 1944 or something like that. I do not have the correct date, but there has been no duty for many, many years.
Since 1944.

Yet we continue to hear that they have paid more. Let us be factual, because they have not paid more for farm machinery. They have paid the same as their American counterparts across the border. They can go over and get it, drive it home or put in on a truck. They can do anything they want. There has been free trade coming into Canada, but there has not been free trade in farm machinery parts, for instance, going into the United States. Farm machinery parts come into Canada free, but going into the United States it was as high as 10 per cent at one time. Even the recent Geneva trade negotiations did not lower the cost of farm machinery parts going into the United States; they did not remove the duty.
The hon. member talked about getting to know the people of Canada, getting out into the country and meeting them. 1 do not think anyone does it any more than I. One of the member's colleagues criticized me the other day for doing just that. I do not find Albertans that much different, that is, the real, ordinary Albertans, the vast majority of Albertans. When they talk about Canada and sharing their resources with the rest of Canada, they are willing to do it. They are willing to do it when it is explained to them properly and honestly. They understand that the resources the federal government takes are the least of any federal system in the world.
Let us make comparisons. The former arrangement for industry was 45 per cent for the provincial government and a magnanimous sum of 10 per cent for the federal government.
November 24, 1980

Was that a tremendous sum? Let us move down to the area south of the border. The hon. member knows as well as I that a lot of the rigs go there because the weather is better for them. It is not just the economic weather about which he talks, but the general trend is the movement of rigs back and forth, a seasonal movement.
Under the new national energy program we are proposing 43 per cent for the provincial government, which is a lessening of the amount by 2 per cent. Certainly that will not greatly lower the billions of dollars or the tremendous amount in the provinces of Alberta or Saskatchewan. We are suggesting the tremendous amount of 24 per cent for the federal government! We are suggesting 33 per cent for the industry.
Now let us move to the state of Texas where they do things really big in their great free enterprise system. In the state of Texas 48 per cent goes to the producers, that is, if one just happens to live above it, 48 per cent goes to the producing company, and 17 per cent goes to the great state of Texas. It is not 43 per cent nor 45 per cent, it is 17 per cent going to the state of Texas, and 35 per cent goes to their federal government. It is not 24 per cent, but 35 per cent that goes to the United States government.
We could move into the other states south of the border and we will see that they never transferred the resources to the states where those rigs go. They practically all belong to the federal government in that area.
Then we could move to a fellow Commonwealth country like Australia. We have talked about the Commonwealth and how we must work together. We have talked about how we have so much in common. Let us talk about the common wealth of these two nations and how they share the common wealth of their own nations. In Australia 37 per cent goes to the producers, 15 per cent to the state government or the equivalent of a provincial government, and 48 per cent to their federal government. That is in the Commonwealth country of Australia. They have something in common with us because we belong to the Commonwealth, but we do not have much in common when it comes to sharing the wealth.
I say to members from western Canada that they should say it like the mayor of Saskatoon did when we were in Saskatoon, Saskatchewan, last Saturday evening. He was talking about sharing when he stood on the platform in front of 750 people at a banquet and said, "No one will rip my country apart. Our country was built by sharing these things in an equitable fashion". That is what the mayor of Saskatoon said when talking about those matters.
Hear, hear!

On Friday I was in Lethbridge talking to a group of farmers, a group of potato growers in the potato commission. When I talked about Canada, they said, "Don't you worry, Mr. Minister, about us. We are Canadians, and we understand because we are people from the rural parts. We understand how this nation was built and we are going to continue to see it done in that fashion".

Hon. members opposite talk about things being done in a unilateral fashion. Let them remember how we transferred the resources to the western provinces-that terrible federal Liberal government did it unilaterally without discussing it with the rest of the provinces! They just handed over the resources.
When we talk about doing some of these things now, like bringing the constitution back, we are bad fellows. But we were good fellows when we transferred the resources unilaterally without discussing it with the other provinces. One province may have objected to it at that time, but the federal government did it in that instance.
I find it difficult to accept some of the remarks of the hon. gentleman when he talked about what is going on. He referred to that "federal group in Ottawa". One would think we did not represent the people of Canada, and one would think that we are holding the money inside the Parliament buildings in some kind of heritage fund and not spreading it around. The federal government's responsibility is to see that there is some economic equity and a distribution of it in the nation For instance, 34 per cent of the federal budget is for social services in Canada. Some members have been suggesting that some parts of Canada will be so much better off because there are no taxes on certain things. They call themselves Canadians within an economic democracy and say that they will have the same economic rights and privileges. They will not have that. Even with the little bit we are suggesting should be shared in a better fashion, one would think we are the destroyers of the free enterprise system.
You said it.

When one checks the multinationals, one will see that they are not sharing as fairly as they will under the policy we are proposing at the present time. So, I do not understand how they can say that it will be the same and that we do not represent the people of Canada.
Let us look at the voting pattern in the province of Alberta. Less than 50 per cent of the people of that province voted in the last election, and less than 50 per cent of them voted for the administration. So, one-quarter of the people with the right to vote voted for the present government of Alberta.
You will be the next minister of finance.

The most socialistic province of all is the province of Alberta. They own more of the land, more of the resources-the airlines and trust companies. Saskatchewan looks like a "little

So when we talk about the energy, the sharing and how we will develop the country and the total energy policy, I return to agriculture where we talk about priorities for energy. It is a difficult thing if you have to have gasoline, diesel fuel or heating fuel for energy in agriculture. These are most important types of fuels and could be the ones that there could be a shortage of in the future.
The total food and beverage industries are classified in one class at the present time. The beverage industry that makes the soft drinks, soda pop, bicarbonated sodas, the wines, the beers and the candy shops-do we give them that high priority classification that we all feel is so necessary for food production on the farm, the primary producer, the food processor and the person who is going to transport the food that you and 1 need? To date, we have heard about energy in its crudest form, and I say that with no pun intended. Canadian farmers have been totally unselfish in their attitude and in the mustering of their energies in order to supply that most important source of energy-food-to their fellow Canadians, for many decades, at reasonable cost. They have performed their tasks efficiently and proficiently to a point at which their achievements are now the envy of the world-and I mean the world, regardless of whether it is communist, socialist, free enterprise, or whatever.
There is no country that works as closely in harmony as we do in providing that source of energy, food, throughout the total food industry. That is probably closer to the true concept of confederation than anything else. It is interesting, when you look at the recommendations about changing the constitution, that not one provincial premier, or the federal government, has recommended any changes when it comes to authority concerning agriculture. It stands for itself that the Fathers of Confederation were far-seeing people who recognized that in order to make a success of it they had to work together.
Since the early 1950s the output for each agricultural worker in Canada has quadrupled, while his or her counterpart in the rest of the commercial sector has only managed to double their output. For example, between 1975 and 1978 the annual rate of growth in labour productivity for farming was a fantastic 4 per cent, while the non-farming sector increased by about 2'A per cent. This has continued. Now the average person who produces food energy for you and me has gone from the point 20 years ago where he only produced enough food to feed approximately 30 people to the point today where he is producing enough food for himself, his family, and 60 other people. If we look at what will happen by the year 2000 we will see that one Canadian farmer will be feeding as many as 150 to 200 people, mainly because of the use of energy.
When we talk about the conservation of energy in the food and beverage industry we see that they have proven to be some of the most conservation-minded people. In the last two years they have cut their energy consumption by 15 per cent, and in the next three to four years they will cut it by another 8 per cent. When we look at how and what we use our energy for, the people in agriculture probably use it more efficiently than any other part of our society. This is argumentative, but I do not mind arguing.
We harvest up to 6 per cent of the world's wheat and barley, 12 per cent of the world's oats, and we produce 2 per cent of the world's meat and milk products. We do not have that much of the world's land. We only have 3 per cent of the world's farmland compared to the world's land resources, yet each of our farmers is more proficient as far as production goes compared with nearly any other country in the world. When you compare our climatic conditions to any other part of the world you will see that we are the most efficient.
If you travel from coast to coast in Canada you will find that the average farmer produces nearly $3,000 worth more of food per farmer than the American farmer. That is going right from Cape Breton Island through to Vancouver Island and Port Hardy.

Not only have our farmers been performing amazing feats in the fields, the work has been accomplished with great energy efficiency as well. Only 3 per cent of the total energy consumed in Canada is used by the agricultural producers, while the car gobbles up more than 25 per cent. It takes equal amounts of energy to produce one pound of wheat as it does one pound of steel. That is taken in the context of planting the seed, tilling the soil, harvesting the crop, processing the product, and getting the product to market. Canadian farmers do not have to apologize to anyone for their use of energy because, compared to their small consumption rate, their contributions to Canada and Canadians are great.
More than 100 years ago eastern farmers laid the groundwork for a national economy. A short time later, western farmers sowed the seed to one of the world's great granaries. The results of their dedication to the Canadian land are now a matter of record, and this tradition, I am sure, has been a source of inspiration to other Canadians from coast to coast.
I believe another one of the major strengths of the Canadian farmer has been the ability to seek security through self-reliance and self-sufficiency, while at the same time working in a spirit of co-operation and unity. These characteristics of selfreliance, self-sufficiency, co-operation, and unity perhaps place the Canadian farmer in a unique position. The amendments to the Petroleum Administration Act have been placed before this House to exact this kind of self-reliance and self-sufficiency for the whole Canadian economy.
Let us take a look at some of the facts. The pricing formula which is being presented now is in no measure as substantial as the increases which were contained in the December, 1979, budget, a move that was supported by the government of that day. In addition, the current amendments to the Petroleum Administration Act contain considerable incentives regarding conservation and alternative energy research.
The Canadian farmers' record for conservation achievement, as I have said, is a record to which one can pay tribute. The Canadian growing season, as hon. members are aware, is short, the climate harsh and the environment at times can play havoc with the orderly growing of our produce. Yet, faced with these odds, the Canadian farmer can still supply Canadian and world markets with food at competitive prices. For example, a tomato grown in a field feeding from the light and heat of nature requires less direct energy than one grown in a greenhouse with artificial light and heat. It takes about $40,000 worth of fuel to maintain one acre of greenhouse and, despite these costs, the Canadian product is still competitive in the market.
Another example is in the area of poultry, such as chickens or turkeys. In warmer environments producers do not need heated buildings or artificial drying procedures for the feed, which is the biggest cost to producers. Although it probably takes one bushel of wheat to prepare a turkey for market, considering the fuel-related additional costs, the Canadian producer is still competitive.
