Many people do not realize that our cattle must be housed longer before they are ready for market. Practically all successful dairymen house their cattle 12 months of the year, leaving them outside only for exercise. The rest of the world is learning our methods in the fields of dairying and poultry. Our methods in poultry are some of the most efficient in the world and can compete on any terms. In spite of our higher costs for wages and energy, we can compete because of our efficiency and marketing ability.
If we are ever to reach self-reliance and self-sufficiency, the key words of the eighties must be conservation and energy alternatives. This perhaps is one area where Canadian farmers are in the most unique position of all, that of being able to produce energy on the farm from low grade wheat, or any product which does not meet the standards of human consumption. Some products, such as manure, can be recycled and, combined with proper conservation, these prospects could, in the very near future, enable the Canadian farmer to snip the umbilical oil cord to foreign supply.
There are many programs sponsored by the government to help people implement their ingenious ideas on energy conservation. Many such projects have been approved by the government as demonstration projects set up by farmers, businessmen, and people in general, who have ideas which they would like to put to good use for Canada. Nobody knows how many of these programs will be successful, but if these people are not given the opportunity to try their ideas we will never know how many of these ideas will be working for us next year or five years from now. Even if one tenth of the hundreds of projects which have been accepted are successful, it would be a tremendous contribution in the field of energy conservation.
Could it be that some day we will be growing energy alternatives as the ultimate resource, because it is a renewable resource? For example, there is wheat. Can we supply the technology to harvest enough energy from one acre, to farm that acre for ten more years while at the same time using the wheat in its traditional form as food? We would simply derive the food from the protein and the energy from the starch. There is also oil from oil seeds and alcohol production from cull crops. In short, it is the ultimate resource that not only fuels the body but would also fuel the technology of the eighties and the nineties. That is the ultimate self-sufficiency and self-reliance. This ultimate goal must be fed by research in order to provide, at a reasonable cost, energy alternatives.
It is in this area of self-sufficiency and conservation I know the Canadian farmer will show leadership to the direct advantage of other Canadians because, on a global scale, rising energy costs will bring about changes and will alter the competitiveness of different farm production and processing enterprises. It only stands to reason that imported foods which have high energy costs in production and transportation will not compete successfully against domestic products. That is another reason why these amendments are important as well as reasonable. They will help our producers use energy efficiently and keep down per unit costs.
Our farmers will be rewarded by a greater share of the domestic and world markets which will produce greater economic advantages. A healthy, growing farm economy means a healthy, growing Canadian economy providing thousands of jobs. At present, one of every four Canadians now works in a food-related job. In addition, every dollar taken in by farming is multiplied by three as it weaves its way through the economy. This year alone the gross farm income will surpass $15 billion. As all hon. members can realize, the impact of the Canadian farmer today is great, and the presence of agriculture in the economy will be felt in the future even more significantly.
1 have drawn a number of parallels, Mr. Speaker, with Canadian agriculture, which include self-reliance, self-sufficiency, the economy, and, indeed, the very essence of development and prosperity, just to name a few. I have tried to offer a Canadian view without the flavouring to suit regional and parochial tastes and to speak on behalf of the Canadian agricultural community which is one element of our great society which spans from coast to coast. As I said earlier, these people perhaps understand and appreciate Canada a little more than many other people in the country.
Neither wheat fields nor livestock herds are restrained by provincial boundaries. All of us in agriculture are proud of our achievements, considering the conditions of adversity such as a northern climate and our battle with the elements which, once again, are a factor that affects all farmers from sea to sea, or for 4,000 miles from coast to coast. The Canadian farming community reaches the very extremities of our land and touches the lives of every Canadian to the benefit of the country. The final parallel, of course, is that the amendments to the Petroleum Administration Act will also reach into the very heartland of our nation touching the lives of every Canadian and benefiting all Canadians.
Canada is one of the greatest countries in the world. We are blessed with our resources, our people, and our tremendous opportunities and energies. The chairman of the American Gas Association who was recently interviewed in a television program in British Columbia, said that Canada has the richest resources of any country in the world. Some hon. members heard me mention my brother the other day. I believe he still belongs to another party. 1 do not know why he belongs to that party, particularly after the way in which he was treated by the Premier of Saskatchewan.
He is the intelligent one of the family.

He was fired.
He tells me not to worry too much about the resources of the provinces because the Northwest Territories and the Yukon have the richest motherload in the world and Canada will remain the richest land and the envy of the entire world. There are tremendous opportunities in Canada. Now is the time for us to extend the spirit of understanding, co-operation, good will and, above all, our unwillingness to surrender our search for a renewed vision of this great country.

Mr. Speaker, I am happy and perhaps a little sad to participate in this debate, in view of its nature. In view of the fact that I follow the ebullient and interesting Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), I should say that I am glad he finally spoke about agriculture and the farmer. I am glad that he mentioned gas and oil too. In view of his opening remarks, and long before he got around to dealing with the farm community and the farm industry, which he does know rather well, his title could have been changed to-and no personal reflection is intended-the "minister of fog" or the "minister of gas". His written remarks were a little more reasonable, rational, and better prepared.
In terms of what the minister said, long before he talked about agriculture, he was trying to answer the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Malone) and others. In this whole debate, Mr. Speaker, there has been, not misrepresentation with intent, but misrepresentation through ignorance or mischief. I do not say the minister tries to mislead the House or anyone outside the House with intent, but the minister speaks in this House about gas and oil, and then fogs the issue by talking
Petroleum Administration Act
about the shares of Texas and Australia! This is a debate on the Petroleum Administration Act. That is what we are trying to talk about in this House. We are trying to register our disapproval of another unilateral move taken by this government which has a central myopia.
This is the first time this has happened in 113 years-in part because this is rather a new bill, I admit. The issue must not be fogged by the use of red herrings and smokescreens, or by the use of false figures. When the minister spoke of the shares he did not mention that in Texas, as in the Commonwealth of Australia, gas revenue is based on federal revenue. It is offshore. When he talked about the shares, the inference was that Alberta was being unduly greedy. I am not here to defend the details of the division of revenue between Alberta and the federal government or the companies, but I find all this most misleading. He pointed out to Alberta that in effect the state of Texas got 17 per cent, compared to Alberta's some 40 per cent, but he did not point out that in Texas, as in Australia, the federal government takes the lion's share because the federal government owns the resource. Until now in this country the resource was owned by the province, and that is where the rub is.
As far as I know, there is no complaint with the figures in Texas or Australia. Maybe they will debate that issue themselves. Under our constitution, however, the resources in the provinces belong to the provinces. That is why, until now, any division of that revenue has been done by agreement, and not by unilaterally invoking the provisions of the Petroleum Administration Act.
I must say, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister of Agriculture wandered even further away from the world of gas and oil when he tried to pervert the history of this land by saying that the four western provinces had made a big land grab, a revenue grab, a resource grab, in effect, in 1930. It was not a Liberal government that was in office at that time, however. I have not quite got it straight whether it occurred before Mr. Bennett came into power or not. I think it was when Mr. Bennett came to power in 1930. The resources were transferred to the four western provinces by an act passed in 1930.
It was not a great gift to those western provinces. They had been fighting for 20 years, ever since they came into confederation in 1905, to obtain the same treatment as every other province. That is the reality, Mr. Speaker, not these red herrings and camouflages and smokescreens and misleading facts that have been dragged into the debate.
In 1930, after 20 years of fighting in the four western provinces, they were put in the same position as all the other provinces in Canada, which was that the resources belonged to the provinces.
Hear, hear!

That is all that was done in 1930. It was not a nefarious plot by those greedy premiers out in the west, way back in 1930. It was not even done by a Liberal government, it was done by the then Conservative government.

The Minister of Agriculture has left the chamber, 1 see. 1 will pay him some respect for his interest in agriculture. That is all I really want to say about the Minister of Agriculture, because I have no disagreement with his remarks about the farmer and the industry and their contributions to the economy of the country. This debate is about the invocation of the Petroleum Administration Act whereby the federal government, for the first time in history, may unilaterally and arbitrarily set the price of oil and gas. This is a brand new situation and it is what the debate is about. It is interesting that it should occur at this time in our national history when we are debating something called the resolution to amend the constitution. I think it can be said objectively that this has created much debate, and certainly division and discord across the country. It is not necessary for the federal government to invoke the Petroleum Administration Act unilaterally in order to set prices now.
I am glad to have the opportunity to speak in this debate, which was prompted by the motions set down by the hon. member for Etobicoke Centre (Mr. Wilson) and, I gather, by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell). Both parties in the opposition are concerned by this unilateral act. This debate is to try to get the government to reconsider. But rather than taking another stick to the west, where the oil and gas are produced, the government should take the extra step and try to reconcile differences.
Following the last meeting in July of this year between the Premier of Alberta and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), the proposals and counterproposals set up then should be used as the base to resolve this problem by agreement rather than having a government act unilaterally. Obviously the numbers game is not in favour of the opposition. The power of numbers is with the government, to move straight ahead. The government may move straight ahead legally and technically, but that still does not say the action it takes tonight is right, or tomorrow, or any other day, because scar tissue is forming across this land.
As my good friend, the hon. member for Richmond-South Delta (Mr. Siddon) has said, it is basically wrong. That is why we are debating this issue today. I must say that a picture speaks a thousand words. I do not know how we can summarize the present state of Canada today in a serious way other than by reminding members of the famous picture which appeared on the front pages of most newspapers last week. I am speaking of our Prime Minister who was off in Saudi Arabia doing the Trudeau tango while this country is in the midst of problems. Never has Canada been more exposed to problems of division and discord with fault on all sides. Another colleague of mine says, "Better away". But, he is the Prime Minister. Picking this time to be offshore when there is a constitutional debate raging across this country, some might say is too pejorative. But now we add to that the debate on the unilateral imposition of prices.
This is the same thing as under a price control bill where the federal government can move and set prices unilaterally within a provincial domain, or set the wages of a worker. It is that type of petty principle that we are talking about when we have the central government moving unilaterally to set the price of gas and oil.
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources in his reply on Friday said, "You have to move some time". With that picture offshore of Rome burning while Nero fiddled, which is analagous to the Prime Minister tangoing while Canada is in the midst of debate, of discord and division, which I do not think has ever occurred before, certainly not in my history as a member of Parliament, I say it is something for which the Prime Minister must take a great deal of responsibility.

I have tried to figure out how we have come to this sorry state, be it on the constitution or here today. I really have to put it down to the federal government which has now been in power for 12 years less eight months. We have a flawed federalism which is blinding the present government to "damn the torpedoes, full speed ahead" action.
The flawed federalism is based on four points. First, it is based on a federal-provincial balance which is out of kilter. Second, it is based on a House of Commons that has never been more unbalanced with regard to representation. Third, it is based on a cabinet of that House of Commons which has never had a more narrow perspective. Fourth, and this ties in with the other three, this has happened at a time in our history when we are moving to "one paper towns". The vacuum created by those one paper towns has been taken up by polls and propaganda, and the manipulation of both.
As far as the first point is concerned, I am not going to cast stones against any one or all the premiers. They together have to accept the blame. The Prime Minister, being Prime Minister of this federal union, obviously has to accept the majority of the blame. Prior to the last several federal-provincial conferences, historically at those conferences there had always been a balance and counterbalance. If the federal government was moving too fast, too far, or too strongly in one direction, historically there was always Quebec and/or Ontario which gave a counterbalance to the strong federal presence that has always been there.
We have heard debates in this House of Commons that this country is too centralized or has never been more decentralized. The fact is that any student of history knows that, depending on the emergency and/or a few wars, regardless of what the Fathers of Confederation felt, certainly with interpretations of the judicial committee of the Privy Council thwarting the original intent of the Fathers of Confederation, the Government of Canada, under any political colouration, has some very strong powers. However, there has always been a counterbalance to the over-use of those powers by the historical counterbalance of the province of Quebec or Ontario, or of both.
Since 1976 and the election of the Parti Quebecois government in Quebec, we no longer have the counterbalance from that province. They, for their reasons, perhaps do not really care what happens to this federal union.
That's not true.

Someone says that is not true. I am talking about the Parti Quebecois government of the province of Quebec. 1 agree I only speak as an outsider, but the government of Quebec does not have its traditional concern to be a counterbalance in a federal union. That government would like to see it changed. There was a referendum in May which was treading on that road.
What I find more difficult to understand, for whatever the reasons, is that the government of Ontario recently has not exercised its historical counterbalance to the federal government moving too far, too fast down a one way street. The two senior partners of confederation, Quebec and Ontario, for their own reasons have not exercised a counterbalance to a strong federal move. Combine that with a new ingredient in the equation of balance, the fact that now in the west there is the emergence of a very real part of this country with an economic clout that demands to be heard, and this has aggravated the situation.
There is the second ingredient of a House of Commons which has never been more unbalanced in representation. The Conservative party has only one member from Quebec. That is obviously not good for the Conservative party or for the country. The government party has only two members west of the Lakehead. That is equally as unbalanced and equally as bad for the country. In addition to that, other than the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen), we do not have a cabinet minister with a strong regional voice to be heard in cabinet circles. This causes an imbalance which allows the Prime Minister to begin on a one-way course.
There is really no one with enough weight or political clout in the cabinet or the House of Commons-there are only two within his ranks-to say, "Whoa, Mr. Prime Minister, are you really helping the nation by invoking the power you may have under the constitution, or are you going to hurt the nation in the long run?" You do not remedy that deficiency in cabinet by appointing some recycled ministers who have no political base in the provinces from which they come, even though they come from the west. That does not help the situation.
The situation is compounded when the only ministers western Canada sees-the active, verbal ministers who deserve a lot of credit-are the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien), the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin). These three ministers are fine Canadians, but their perspective of the country comes from a narrow base.
One province.

I say that in an objective way, because all three of those ministers are personal friends of mine. There was a meeting at the weekend in Saskatoon or Regina at which the Minister of Justice spoke about the flag debate. The constitutional debate cannot be compared with the flag debate. 1 will not go off on that red herring, but if the minister has to invoke the flag debate to justify moving unilaterally on the constitution or the Petroleum Administration Act, then he and the government are in a really sick, sad state.
November 24, 1980

Unfortunately, I suppose that my time is almost up. I will conclude. When we have these ingredients in a federal-provincial system, which 1 think is out of balance historically, and when we have a House of Commons which is out of balance in representation and a cabinet which comes from too narrow a base, and we put those together-

subsubtopic: VOLUNTARY AGENCIES SUGGESTED ADDITIONAL GOVERNMENTAL AID
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of providing volunteer agencies with financial aid to support their communication and fund-raising activities, so that a greater portion of available funds could be freed for their intended charitable uses.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in speaking to this motion I want to define its terms. I recognize the reality of the present day where, in the face of the budget, inflation and rising costs, it is unrealistic to urge and press the government to add additional dollars to existing grants to voluntary agencies through a variety of government channels.
This afternoon I am proposing that financial aid be given in equivalents of goods and services. It will not cost the federal government more dollars and it will make use of facilities already in place by using them during non-peak periods.
Recently the hon. member for Edmonton South (Mr. Roche) proposed that the $ 100-deduction be eliminated so that individuals would be encouraged to give more to voluntary agencies. I agree with that proposal and would like to see it go further, to the point where voluntary agencies would enjoy the same tax benefits as political parties. Today, however, I am advocating that the government should pursue the direction recommended by its own Advisory Council on Voluntary Action. In these difficult days the government should provide tangible assistance to offset a number of the fixed costs which voluntary agencies must bear.
It is important to note that such a proposal would seem timely. During times of high unemployment and inflation, there is an increase in the number of people who are in need of care and support. Government resources are already stretched to the limit and there is a question concerning their allotment. Taxpayers have less disposable income, and there is more competition for available voluntary donations.
Another factor which makes it timely is rampant inflation. Many people who formerly could give many hours of voluntary work are now seeking places in the work force, thereby putting increased pressure on available volunteer leadership. The recent budget, with its lack of any offsets for those least able to pay, will dramatically increase the overhead costs of voluntary agencies, due to large increases in UIC payments for core
November 24, 1980
staff and across-the-board energy increases which will affect the heating of their offices and staff travel.
I speak with concern for this sector of our society arising out of my own experience for a number of years with CUSO in its formative years, as a field officer in West Africa and as a co-ordinator of the Canadian and Manitoba centennials. Also, I directed a small voluntary international agency. I continue to sit as a board member of several agencies and councils. I remember the early days of CUSO when goods and services were made available to send volunteers to developing countries. Canadian Air Force aircraft were made available, as were telex and health services.
The direction I am proposing the federal government should take is not in any way new. There has long been a feeling in the country of the importance of the balance among the private, public and voluntary sectors and of the need for recognition of the contribution voluntary agencies make to the life of the nation.
As early as 1951 the Royal Commission on Arts, Letters and Sciences, which published the Massey report, looked at the importance of voluntary societies. In part the report indicated:
The voluntary society has played an important part in modern history, from the religious sects and the salons of the seventeenth century, through the political clubs of the revolutionary era, down to the nineteenth century with its innumerable organizations to aid, prevent, propagate or promote every conceivable end.
We have the fine tradition of the voluntary society which performs work of national importance beyond what the government can or will do.
The Massey report indicated that a special problem of the local society is the scantiness of the Canadian population. It continued:
We were, therefore, interested to see in several different cities a special kind of voluntary association. This is the "Council" representing a variety of organizations, each leading its separate existence, but combining for some common purpose.
The Massey report called for more co-operation between voluntary agencies and government in a "more generous and flexible way". This is the direction 1 wish to impress upon the government this afternoon.
Following on from the affirmation displayed in the Massey report, the Trudeau government set up a National Advisory Council on Volunteerism. Its report will be familiar to the members of the House. It was entitled "People in Action", and was published in 1977. In part it indicated that there was:
-a need for greater awareness of, and increased commitment to, voluntary activity by both government and the general public.
I should like to quote some excerpts from the report which was tabled in the House but not acted upon. It read:
Voluntary action is "active" citizenship. It is people accepting a real responsibility for shaping their communities and their country and acting in some way on that responsibility.
It continued:
The most obvious form of non-financial assistance is aid-in-kind. This includes access to government facilities, premises, resources, efforts to improve the responsiveness of government personnel to voluntary action and various types of non-financial support services.
November 24, 1980

However, aid-in-kind could be effectively provided at relatively little cost if clear guidelines existed for supplying this assistance.
It went on:
In particular, the government should focus on ways in which it could help voluntary associations overcome the vast distances and geographical barriers separating so many Canadian communities-
It is very costly to communicate or travel between different communities separated by such distances.
In another section the report recommended that:
The Department of the Secretary of State, in collaboration with a committee of voluntary associations, study the best way to implement special measures to help voluntary associations overcome physical barriers to communication.
More specifically, the government should consider how to render such government communications facilities as WATS telephone lines and telex accessible to voluntary associations at no or limited cost. In the area of transportation, the department and the committee should examine how best to ensure that the economies of charter and excursion flights can be made available to members of voluntary associations attending their annual conventions and meetings-
Most voluntary associations depend extensively on the circulation of printed materials to their memberships because, unlike government and business, voluntary associations do not have access to such facilities as WATS lines or telex. Most voluntary associations also cannot afford such facilities, and long distance telephone calls over normal lines can be prohibitively expensive in any quantity-
The council believes that the solution lies in a special reduction in postal rates for the informational materials and publications of voluntary associations. The government already keeps track of many voluntary associations through their registration as "charities" by Revenue Canada. Accordingly, the council recommends that:
The federal government grant a special postal rate for mailing of publications and informational materials by all voluntary associations registered with Revenue Canada.
It continued:
All of Canada's human resources are needed in a time when the realization is dawning that resources are not inexhaustible and that hard times may be ahead. In an environment of concern and support by government, voluntary action could ensure that the diversity of Canadian society is an enriching rather than a fragmenting force. Thus, government should strengthen rather than diminish its support for voluntary action. The problems of this country cannot be solved if people cannot utilize their own tools and resources, cannot participate in decisions from time to time through their own voluntary associations ... Government should not create counter-associations to serve its own interests. Rather, it should let the people confront important issues with their own initiatives and resources and through their own voluntary associations.
Indeed, the people involved in voluntary action constitute a vital, multipurpose human resource.
Mr. Speaker, I am asking that this House request the government to provide to the voluntary sector, which is hard-pressed during these days of rising costs and cutbacks, practical assistance in terms of rail travel in the regions of our country and air travel on a standby or special designation basis between the vastly separated parts of our country. I ask for assistance in terms of computer time, which can help agencies keep in touch with their volunteers, and collect their resources. Translation services, the increased use of the CBC facilities and other cable network facilities, the vastly expanded use of government meeting rooms and facilities, use of telephone service on a restricted basis in off-peak periods, are ways to assist the voluntary sector. They could use assistance in terms of printing facilities which are located in regions across the
Voluntary Agencies
country. They need postal assistance, as outlined in the report of the National Advisory Council on Voluntary Action.
Voluntary agencies from my riding have given me a number of helpful suggestions.They have emphasized to me the importance of maintaining their networks in the communities and across the country. They have emphasized to me the difficulty of obtaining and maintaining equipment. For example, the Kitchener-Waterloo Global Centre wrote a letter to me as follows:
Could we make arrangements to use duplicating equipment which most government offices have available? Even if we had to supply our own paper, our costs would be greatly reduced with the free use of such equipment. What about other equipment-slide/tape, video, etc.?
We would also appreciate access to meeting rooms and office space. The latter would be especially useful when we have specific time-limited projects under way. What does the government do with used furniture and office equipment?
The Waterloo Region Chapter of the Canadian Mental Health Association in a letter asked:
Could some tax incentive be worked out for people who volunteer time as well as for people who donate money?
Mr. Speaker, in these comments and in citing this historical background I am urging the government to look favourably upon a concept set forth in the Massey report advocated by its own Advisory Council on Voluntary Action. The questions which will be immediately raised by those who are concerned about bureaucratic structures and the functioning of this type of proposal are how decisions will be made, who will decide what can be done, by whom and when.
I suggest to you there are a number of co-ordinating councils across our nation. In the international development area I have in mind the Canadian Council for International Co-operation, in the area of international education the Canadian Bureau for International Education, the Canadian Council on Social Development, the Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops and the Canadian Council of Churches in terms of our Christian community and the Canadian Jewish Council in terms of their community. There are many other councils of a multicultural nature and others which draw our communities together. I am suggesting that a mechanism be set up to consult with them about ways and means of using the existing resources. These are resources which are already in place and which are already being paid for by the Canadian taxpayers.
In these days of big government and of increased inflation and financial hardship, there are a great many people across our land who are in danger of finding themselves without the caring structures that are needed. These smaller and more personalized individual agencies provide an inspiration, motivation, and a caring focus to our community. I suggest that action of this order would not only be economically appropriate to the times in which we live but it would also be one which takes seriously the social fabric of our nation.
Mr. Speaker, thank you for the opportunity of presenting this motion for the consideration of this House.

speakeroldname: Mr. John Evans (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: VOLUNTARY AGENCIES SUGGESTED ADDITIONAL GOVERNMENTAL AID
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in discussing this motion I am sure there will be no disagreement on one point, that is, the importance of voluntary agencies within our Canadian society. 1 do not think there can be any doubt about that importance. Through these voluntary groups citizens can focus their efforts on problems that really concern them. The ability of these groups to act promptly and effectively could well be emulated by government bureaucracies. Throughout the years, voluntary agencies have been the spearhead for many important social changes in our society. If we did not have a voluntary sector, Mr. Speaker, I am quite confident that we would have to think of what the quality of life in our society might be like.
This is the second time in this Parliament that we have been asked to consider the financial health of the charitable and voluntary organizations in our society. On June 9 the House debated the motion of the hon. member for Edmonton South (Mr. Roche) relating to tax deductions for charitable donations. The proposal at that time involved a rather substantial increase in tax revenues forgone so as to provide greater incentive to charitable giving. Because of the large cost involved there was no agreement at that time on the preferable policy which would be followed.
With today's motion by the hon. member for Waterloo (Mr. McLean) we have another proposal that would involve a new charge on the treasury. Given what the hon. member has said in elaboration on the nature of his proposal, I suggest that that charge on the treasury could be substantial indeed. Moreover, the prospective financial burden is a very indefinite one. Certainly by reading the motion that the hon. member has submitted I was originally of the opinion that the government would be asked to provide certain rather limited services for communication and fund-raising activities, to use the terms of the motion. Yet when 1 hear now what the hon. member has in mind I find that it is a much broader scope of activities and services.
The motion does not stipulate how much financial aid might be required of the federal government. It does not make clear how widely this program of federal grants would be applied. In other words, what kind of voluntary agencies would qualify? How many might be involved and what kind of guidelines would apply to these federal outlays?
I suggest that even with the best will in the world, and with the greatest of sympathy and understanding for the voluntary sector and its importance to our society, we still have a responsibility to examine some of these issues, if not all. In considering a proposal like this we might well look to the Speech from the Throne for one guiding principle which I suggest is relevant here. This guiding principle is:
That Canadians recognize the need to live within their national means, and they understand that in doing so the state cannot meet every demand or satisfy every group. Therefore, in employing the limited resources available, my ministers will help first those who need help most.
Obviously there is no shortage of good causes which appeal to our sympathy and to the federal treasury. But there is also a shortage of funds available to assist them. We must have a very lively concern for the size of the federal deficit. We should be aware of what federal aid is already being provided in this area. And we should be very careful about assessing the financial implications of making bold and generous declarations of principle in favour of helping this or that worthy cause.
The extent of federal support for voluntary, charitable organizations and causes is already substantial. In income tax alone the amount of revenue forgone annually by federal and provincial governments as a result of deductions for charitable givings is estimated at $600 million. The public accounts are sprinkled with references to grants to a wide variety of voluntary agencies. An excellent example is the New Horizons program under which some $11 million is made available for projects by voluntary groups of older citizens aimed at helping themselves and their community. There are many other examples of federal support for worth-while voluntary endeavours.
I suggest that, for all practical purposes, the government is already doing a great deal of what is proposed in this motion. Admittedly, federal grants are not earmarked in support of communication and fund-raising activities of these voluntary agencies, as the motion proposes. But I think it is obvious that, for the organization involved, the contribution is the important thing and not how it might be earmarked.
For that reason I find it rather difficult to understand why the hon. member for Waterloo has specified in his motion that the federal assistance be directed toward communication and fund-raising activities, so as to free up the funds of the voluntary group for its charitable goals. Surely the distinction is a meaningless one in terms of the way voluntary agencies operate. In fact, if any distinction is to be made, I suggest that a better case could be made for earmarking the federal grant for a particular social purpose, thereby making use of the energy, expertise and flexibility of voluntary agencies to achieve a goal that both the agency and the government desire. As I have indicated, that sort of approach is already being followed in a good many federal grants.
I would like to turn to another issue that is raised by the terms of this motion. That is the problem of defining which voluntary agencies are to qualify for the proposed federal assistance. The motion is not clear as to whether the government should have discretion in deciding which agencies receive these proposed grants, or whether some blanket assistance program is to be made available to all agencies that meet a given set of criteria. If it is the latter, then I suggest we could be opening up a very wide door into the federal treasury.
This problem of defining what is a voluntary agency can be a most difficult and vexing one. Let me illustrate by reference to the government's past experience with the deductibility allowed under the Income Tax Act for donations to registered charities. As hon. members can imagine, it is a matter of great importance for a charity whether or not it can qualify as a
November 24, 1980

registered charity and thus be able to issue tax-deductible receipts to its financial supporters.
There is no legal definition of a "charity" for tax purposes. In deciding whether a charity is to be registered, Revenue Canada now uses the common law classification of charitable purposes. Three of these purposes are fairly specific: the relief of poverty, the advancement of education, and the advancement of religion. The fourth category is a general one: other activities beneficial to the community. In fact, however, this category of charitable purposes has been subjected in the courts to a fairly restricted common law interpretation which has limited the range of organizations able to qualify as charities. Another general requirement which all organizations must meet is that their activities must be concerned with the benefit of the public or of a large section of the public. The result of all of this is that some 40,000 charities are registered and qualify as the recipients of tax-deductible donations.
Suggestions have been made that a legal definition of charity should be drawn up so as to give a wider meaning to the term, and in this way to reflect better the wide variety of activities carried out by voluntary groups in our modern society. It is argued that we need more clearcut criteria for deciding what is to qualify as a charity. In fact, however, the task of redefining just what constitutes a charity would be a good deal more complex than it might seem. And when we remind ourselves that already more than half a billion dollars in tax revenues are forgone through tax deductions for charitable purposes, we should be very cautious about the possibility of opening even wider the door to this particular kind of tax deduction.
Apart from the legal issue, there are some quite pragmatic justifications for the inclusion of some charities among Revenue Canada's registered charities, and the exclusion of others. For example, national sports organizations are included, but not provincial and local sports bodies. In our federal system I think that makes sense. It is reasonable that, for sports at this level, provincial and local governments be expected to provide the kind of financial support that their electorate feels is justified.
I realize that the motion, as worded, does not limit its scope to those registered charities recognized by Revenue Canada. It refers, instead, to voluntary agencies. But the very same kind of definitional problems would arise in any program of government grants. The questions are not easy. First, what kind of activities would qualify? Second, would the voluntary agency be required to devote a certain minimum of its revenues to charitable purposes, and if so how much? Third, would there be any criteria as to the minimum number of persons benefiting from the charity? And finally, what standards of public accountability would be required?
Some may think that this suggests a lot of undesirable government interference in the activities of voluntary groups. Obviously, that is a danger. There are some philosophical questions which might be asked; such as, how far can a voluntary agency go in seeking government help before it loses its essentially voluntary character and becomes just another
Voluntary Agencies
agency of government? But that is a question the agencies must ask themselves. As members of Parliament, we must concern ourselves with questions about priorities in government spending, and about proper controls on the way federal funds are spent.
Although I share the concern of the hon. member for Waterloo about the importance of a strong and vigorous voluntary sector, I am forced to the conclusion that his motion leaves too many of these essential questions without adequate answers. After listening to the hon. member I became even more concerned in this regard because he indicated that this motion, contrary to my interpretation of the wording, would involve assistance from the government. I am not sure here if we are talking only about the federal government or if we are talking about the federal government and the provincial governments and the municipalities.
The hon. member referred to such services as reproduction services which may or may not include provision for the reproducing paper. The program may involve free mailing service through Canada Post. If the government is to become involved in this kind of program, it must ask some fairly basic questions. When an agency of the government is established, it is through a parliamentary process or some action of Parliament. Presumably that agency is established for a specific purpose related to public policy. A question would arise with regard to particular voluntary agencies which spring up of their own accord. These agencies do not necessarily spring up as a result of some specific policy purpose which has been widely recognized by the population.
As a result, irrespective of how we define voluntary groups or how we define the services that the government or governments are expected to provide to these voluntary groups, the taxpayers of Canada are expected to contribute to their financing through a program such as this. Under this program, all voluntary groups would presumably have equal and free access to a wide range of service from the government, from the public purse. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that if those agencies or groups are established as a result of debate and the clear definition of a public policy purpose, that is one thing. Then the taxpayers, it seems to me, can be asked to support, in a very broad way, the activities of these groups. Certainly that question does arise in connection with the tax deductibility of groups and we have defined certain of the groups for tax purposes in my speech to this point.
The question that arises is whether we now intend to allow unlimited access to the public treasury by a large, large number of associations which can be instituted and established on their own volition. If that is the case, it seems to me a great deal of control over the public purse would be lost. More important, Mr. Speaker, we would be asking all the taxpayers of Canada to support, in a very direct way, a wide range of voluntary organizations which they themselves might not otherwise wish to support. I agree they are now being asked to do this as a result of the tax deductibility clause in the tax
5008

November 24, 1980
Voluntary Agencies
system. If I give to a voluntary organization which qualifies as a charity I can write that donation off against my taxes. As a result, all taxpayers are effectively paying the additional tax load to make up for the amount I am not paying as a result of the tax deduction I have received.
I think the motion would take this much further, Mr. Speaker, and would loosen the controls which now exist with regard to voluntary organizations. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, when we realize just how broad the services to be provided under this particular motion would be, that the whole question has to be debated carefully and at great length because under this motion we would be imposing a substantial financial burden on the taxpayers of the country-one which is not well defined in the motion; it is not well defined with regard to the organizations which would qualify to receive this assistance, that is voluntary organizations, as opposed to charitable organizations. To me a voluntary organization means any organization that conducts its business through the efforts of voluntary workers. That is a voluntary organization. I am not being paid for doing a job, I am volunteering my services, therefore I am part of a voluntary organization. Clearly, Mr. Speaker, that definition is so broad as to make this motion unacceptable from a public policy point of view and certainly unacceptable from a tax point of view.
The second issue is the breadth of the services which would be available to these groups under the motion. As I said earlier, Mr. Speaker, I was of the very strong opinion that the services to which these groups would have access were relatively limited. The motion reads as follows:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of providing volunteer agencies with financial aid to support their communication and fund-raising activities, so that a greater portion of available funds could be freed for their intended charitable uses.
However, when the hon. member for Waterloo (Mr. McLean) put forward his list of what he considers to be "for the purposes of communications and fund-raising support", it turned out to be much more comprehensive than I ever anticipated it would be.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, there appears to be some confusion in the motion itself. The first part refers to volunteer agencies and then at the end it refers to the intended charitable uses.

speechtext: The hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Halliday).

subsubtopic: VOLUNTARY AGENCIES SUGGESTED ADDITIONAL GOVERNMENTAL AID
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I want to congratulate the hon. member for Waterloo (Mr. McLean) for bringing this motion forward for debate today. As mentioned previously, this is the second time it has been up for consideration this session, which indicates the concern members feel with respect to the social policies now being put forward by this government.
We in the official opposition have been rather pleased by the addition of the hon. member for Waterloo to our party and to his membership in the House of Commons because he brings to this House the type of social conscience which has been missing from the government side for too many years. We are
sometimes asked, particularly at election time, what the difference is between the Conservative party and the Liberal party. Some people find themselves hard pressed to find an answer, but I think one could say, Mr. Speaker, that a difference is apparent here today. The difference is that we, on this side, recognize that these social problems exist and want to see them solved by the organizations and the people themselves.
There has been strong tendency on the part of the Liberal government to adopt the principle that if there is a social problem, the government should take over and fix it. That is what we are trying to get away from. I think the people of Canada want to see themselves involved in solving these social problems.
The motion which the hon. member for Waterloo has put forward reads as follows:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of providing volunteer agencies with financial aid to support their communication and fund-raising activities, so that a greater portion of available funds could be freed for their intended charitable uses.
The hon. member for Waterloo has indicated that he is looking at this in a perspective which acknowledges that there are financial constraints on governments in times such as these and we are not asking for more money, per se. We want more assistance, which is equivalent to financial assistance. The hon. member for Waterloo has directed attention to a number of the types of services which could be rendered. 1 grant the fact that there is a small pecuniary involvement in some of the services which might be provided, but in terms of large grants, the hon. member for Waterloo was not asking for large sums of money.
I listened with interest to the parliamentary secretary, Mr. Speaker. He spoke well and he touched on some of the problems that the government faces in trying to provide more funding. I was a little disappointed and a little surprised- although upon reflection I should not have been-that he did not refer once to the very significant document to which the hon. member for Waterloo referred. "People in Action" is a document on voluntary organizations commissioned by the government a few years ago. A report was made to the Secretary of State in September, 1977, and I am sure that if the government felt it had implemented any of the 81 recommendations in that report, the parliamentary secretary would have told us about it this afternoon. That is what the government usually does-it talks about all the recommendations it has implemented.
Mr. Speaker, I assume that they have not implemented any. Not one in the past three years! I think we should look at those recommendations to see what the government has failed to do by way of implementing a report which it commissioned and asked for. We have raised the question of the lack of funds and the report acknowledges this problem. It contains a chapter on the nature of government's responsibility. At page 138 the following sentence appears.
It will be important for government, not necessarily to spend more money, but to spend existing funds in different ways.
November 24, 1980

The parliamentary secretary was speaking a few minutes ago about priorities of government spending. That is exactly what is suggested here, that we have to consider priorities in government spending. I want to say a few words about a possible shift in those priorities, to support a suggestion made in this report, that not necessarily is it important to spend more money. Recommendation No. 34 reads:
The federal government affirm in principle and through policy its responsibility to safeguard the basic freedoms of action and association through creating conditions within which Canadian citizens are enabled, encouraged and assisted to act voluntarily about those matters which concern them.
Recommendation 35 is even more significant. It recommends that-
Government ensure that voluntary associations have equal access to grants and other means of support-
That is exactly what the hon. member for Waterloo (Mr. McLean) is suggesting, that voluntary associations should have other means of support in addition to financial means. Recommendation No. 35 continues-
-equal opportunity to make their voices heard and the means to emerge and develop in accordance with their own needs, concerns and priorities.
Further along in this report, at page 253, a whole chapter is devoted to what is headed "Non-Financial Support". We are suggesting the government should have taken a look at this, but it has failed to do so. I will read from the first paragraph in reference to the non-Financial relationships which could exist if we had a government that really cared.
These involve general support, the bestowal of recognition and the release of information. A fourth type-consultative relationships-will be discussed in chapter 13.
As this concept of general support is dealt with, the council talks about some of the problems which exist now and the help voluntary organizations might receive to further their goals. They talk about the need for public access to the information which the government has. At page 268 another recommendation is found. I will read it because it is most apropos. It is recommendation No. 74, which reads as follows:
Access-to-information legislation be enacted by the Parliament of Canada creating a statutory right of persons to obtain access to information held by the government or its agencies, subject only to a list of narrowly defined exceptions, with any refusal to provide such information and any unreasonable delay or costs subject to review and enforcement by the courts on the merits, with burden of proof on the government.
They are asking for what I hope we will see from this government eventually, that is, an opportunity for Canadians to receive the information they need-in the case of voluntary organizations, that they receive the information they need to pursue their activities. This report contained another recommendation in 1977-1978 that the government inaugurate a voluntary action resource centre. So far nothing at all has been done about that. In recommendation No. 75, it is suggested that annual reports be provided by various departments so that voluntary associations would be able to know what was available in the public sector for their use.
Before I close, I want to touch on the matter the parliamentary secretary raised regarding the priorities the government
Voluntary Agencies
has to follow in these days of limited funds for spending. We have become quite used to the concept of universality in all our social programs in Canada. I was pleased a year or so ago when the present government, then in opposition, talked about the need to help those who need help most. During the election campaign we heard the Prime Minister and others speaking on that same topic stress the importance of helping those Canadians who most need help. This runs quite counter to the concept of universality in all social programs.
A number of us in the House have recently had the opportunity of serving on a special committee known as the Special Committee for the Disabled and the Handicapped. We have had occasion to listen to dozens of briefs from dozens of voluntary organizations of the type to which the member from Waterloo has been referring. We are well aware of the problems these people have. It has been brought to our attention very acutely that large sectors of the Canadian population are not adequately being taken care of. In fact, they are not being given the very basics to which most of us in this House think Canadians are entitled. I am suggesting, without anticipating the recommendation in the committee's report which has yet to come, that we as representatives of the Canadian people must consider doing something for Canadians who are underprivileged in some special way, such as those who are handicapped and disabled. As things are, we are not even giving them the very basics. For instance, we are not making any effort as Canadians to see that persons whose mobility is limited are given an equal opportunity to move around. I could go on to talk about those who have vision impairments, hearing impairments, and so on. Voluntary organizations looking for help from this Parliament, and this government in particular, are not necessarily demanding more money. But they are demanding that the government take a second look at its priorities, as I hope the parliamentary secretary was suggesting a little while ago. Possibly the time has come when some of us who receive funds from the government regularly or who have things done by the government on our behalf although we are quite able to pay for them, should now be saying that those who are more handicapped or who enjoy fewer privileges in one way or another should be getting top priority for a little while. As I say, we should be taking a look at the priorities of government and reassessing some of the needs.
I think the hon. member for Waterloo in bringing forth this very commendable motion today is telling us that the government does have the funds, but one way or the other the funds are not being directed where they should be. The government has at its disposal facilities and services which could be utilized by voluntary organizations. Moreover, funds are being spent on people who do not need help just because the service is universal. This money could better be used by and on behalf of people who need it more. While the government might take exception to some of the wording in this motion, I hope it will recognize the importance of the concept which lies behind it. I hope the motion will be allowed to pass so that it may be debated in committee.

November 24, 1980
Voluntary Agencies

Mr. Speaker, I should like to join with my friend, the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Halliday), in commending the hon. member for Waterloo (Mr. McLean) for bringing this motion before the House this afternoon.

speechtext: They are nil.

subsubtopic: VOLUNTARY AGENCIES SUGGESTED ADDITIONAL GOVERNMENTAL AID
speechtext:
But at least we are having a discussion of the subject, and 1 hope the discussion will play its part in persuading the government to review more seriously its attitude toward voluntary organizations.
There can be no doubt as to the important part voluntary organizations have played in our society for decades, indeed for centuries, and there is still an important part for them to play. I believe the people of Canada want to see voluntary organizations given every break that can possibly be given to them. At the same time, 1 should like to say that every time this discussion comes up I get a little uneasy about the efforts which some people make to try to play the voluntary sector and the public off against one another. As I see it, the main contribution of the voluntary organizations is that they have been pioneers. They have persuaded society that something should be done to help less (fortunate members of our society. But as time has gone on, it has become necessary for the public, for the state-the government-to take over these services. The fact is that today I have heard figures as high as 95 per cent. Certainly it is 90 per cent or more of the services which are provided by the government to those who need them. One thinks of such things as housing, health and education. Where would we be today in these areas if this had been left to the voluntary organizations? The government has had to move in.
Then there is the whole question of the maintenance of family income with various kinds of supports. There is the situation which faces our senior citizens, not only in terms of pensions on which to live, but recreation, accommodation, home care and all the rest. As a matter of fact, today voluntary organizations are pioneering in fields such as greater home care, child care and so on. If I had time-and I do not want to be the one to talk this out-I could list things that were done by the voluntary or private organizations when I came here, which was a number of years ago, and which have been taken over.
I do not believe we should play one against the other. In my view, the important thing for some of us to push for is greater public involvement in such matters as security and all the rest which are needed for our senior citizens to improve the lot of those who should be maintained in their own homes, in day care for children and all the rest. Let us not pit one against the other. Both are vitally important.
In the context of this afternoon's motion, it is good for us to realize that even though the public service may be taking care of 90 per cent or 95 per cent of the problems the other 5 per cent or 10 per cent need to be looked at as well. In addition, there is still a pioneering job to be done. It is on that basis I express the hope that the government will give serious consideration to the thrust of the proposal made in the motion before us this afternoon.

speakeroldname: Mr. Roy MacLaren (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: VOLUNTARY AGENCIES SUGGESTED ADDITIONAL GOVERNMENTAL AID
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to have the honour to speak in this debate because the hon. member for Waterloo (Mr. McLean) and I had the opportunity to serve together on a voluntary organization, the Canadian Council for International Co-operation, some years ago. At that time I learned to admire his genuine concern for those in our society, both at home and in other countries, who are deprived or underprivileged. The concern of which he gave such evidence on those occasions is certainly reflected in the bill before us this afternoon.
Other members from both sides of this House have paid tribute to the hon. member's motives in bringing forward this matter today. I want to share in the expression of concern which is reflected in the bill. It is a concern that voluntary organizations, which can play such a substantial part in our society, should have access to the resources, whether they come from the private sector or in part from the public, to enable them to carry out their important functions, both at home and abroad.
In his motion concerning aid for voluntary organizations, the hon. member for Waterloo addresses a function that is important, perhaps in some sense vital, to a free society: the dynamic and ever-changing human activity whereby individuals, or groups of individuals, contribute of their own volition to the betterment of themselves, their communities and their country.
Voluntary organizations are not necessarily similar in their aims and philosophies. Some lend support to traditional values in our society; others are in the vanguard of change. Yet their very diversity is indicative of the vigour of our society and of the great desire of many of us to work for the general well-being of others.
The government is well aware of the valuable services provided by the voluntary sector to which it continues to give a variety of aid and encouragement. The Department of the Secretary of State, for example, administers a number of programs which provide aid to voluntary groups operating in certain fields of interest. These include the changing role of women in society, the progress of native citizens in today's world, human rights, and ethnocultural groups which honour their past while adapting to life in Canada.
The importance given in the motion to communications is well considered. The National Advisory Council on Voluntary Action to the Government of Canada paid special attention to the difficulties faced by a national voluntary organization in maintaining communications.
November 24, 1980

The hon. member and I recall that most voluntary associations depend extensively on the circulation of printed materials to their membership because, unlike government and business, they do not have every access to such facilities as wide area long distance telephone service or telex. Most voluntary associations could not afford such facilities, and long distance telephone calls over normal lines can be prohibitively expensive in any quantity. Thus, in order to maintain adequate and efficient communications with their members, voluntary associations are forced to restrict themselves to mail service. There is no alternative for them and the effects of continually rising postal rates can be very serious, not only in strictly financial terms, but also because they force some associations to rely on bulk mailings which have a low priority in the post office.
The Advisory Council proposed a plan that would help qualified associations to make good use of the mails. Noting that voluntary associations may be registered as charitable organizations by Revenue Canada, it was suggested that the federal government grant a special postal rate for mailing of publications and informational materials by all voluntary associations so registered.
Other measures of support and encouragement are provided by the government, but before continuing I should like to express a concern which I have with regard to this motion. I do not feel we shall best serve the voluntary sector by supporting specific areas of activity such as, in this instance, communications and fund raising. Some of these independent organizations, serving different needs in different regions and circumstances, may identify other needs that they find more urgent. It is my conclusion, and that of the voluntary organizations themselves, that the most appropriate, the most useful, role of government is to create an environment which would encourage members of the public to make donations in support of the voluntary actions of which they approve. One interesting proposal currently before the government is to change the present tax regulations, which provide little incentive for charitable gifts except among richer citizens, so that all could have similar tax savings by virtue of charitable gifts.
Before speaking further on this tax proposal, Mr. Speaker, 1 should like to refer to a special quality of voluntary groups which it would be well to consider. Generally speaking, "voluntarism" is the independent action of an individual or a group to bring about what are seen as desirable changes in society. It therefore seems important to the viability and, indeed, the validity, of a voluntary association that it not rely too heavily on direct government aid lest it lose its independent spirit-
