speechtext: When the debate was interrupted at five o'clock the hon. member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan (Mr. McRae) had the floor.

Mr. Speaker, to recapitulate for a moment, I was discussing what I have observed over many years, particularly when we were dealing with a series of energy bills over the last years and particularly in the national resources committee of which I have been a member during those years. We on this side have tended to be in the middle with the New Democratic Party pushing for more and the Conservative party saying we had done too much.
This pattern has developed over the years. The New Democrats have taken a very strong stand with regard to the Petroleum Administration Act, and I read a quotation from the remarks of Tommy Douglas, their energy critic, supporting the bill strongly and saying that prices should not go higher. There was no vote on that bill at any of its readings, but it always passed on division with the New Democrats supporting it.
I am surprised that the New Democratic Party should now take an opposite stand to that which it has taken all along. I think there is a real contradiction in this area. I also suggest that there are one or two other contradictions.
I mentioned the genuine concern my party has traditionally had for underdeveloped countries; the Prime Minister is out of the country for a series of reasons but one very strong reason has to do with the North-South dialogue.
I will not spend too much time on this, but before we adjourned the debate at five o'clock I did mention something which disturbs me very much because 1 think it marks a real departure from traditional NDP policy. The Leader of the New Democratic Party went to Newfoundland and once again laid out the idea that offshore resources should be owned and controlled by the province. That is a recent policy of his party, and I think it is a very strange move. To my mind it has always been traditional among progressives whether in Canada, the United States, Britain or wherever that the smaller the juris-
*

Petroleum Administration Act
diction the easier it is for multinational corporations to control that jurisdiction. If control over offshore resources were in the hands of the province of Newfoundland it would be much easier for it to shift into the hands of very large multinational corporations. I think it has always been the tradition of the New Democratic Party that a strong central government is necessary in this country. Evidently there is a diversion from that tradition.
This evening I would like to try to put myself-I have been trying to do this over the last six months or a year-into the shoes of an Albertan who was born and grew up in Alberta. In some ways I can understand the way many Albertans must feel. I grew up in Toronto and moved later in my life to Thunder Bay where I spent a good portion of my adult life. Thunder Bay is in many ways as distant from Toronto and the southern Ontario horseshoe as is Alberta, and I do not mean geographically. I am talking in terms of differences in outlook. At least part of my riding is in Thunder Bay, and at this time it is fairly affluent, perhaps even more affluent than some areas of southern Ontario. I cannot believe the people of Thunder Bay or the people of Alberta are feeling the way they are feeling out of greed, I just cannot accept that. I was interested in what the hon. member for Annapolis Valley-Hants (Mr. Nowlan) had to say because I think he was saying basically the same thing. There are always people who will do things out of greed in any society, but generally speaking I do not think that is the situation here.
If I had lived in Alberta in the 1920s or 1930s, I could understand the tough years when Alberta was a kind of hinterland to the east or to central Canada where there was a lot of wealth, development and growth. I could understand the tariff approaches and so on. This would be in my mind as an Albertan. I would feel strongly that over the years Albertans had been "had" by the centre of the country, particularly Ontario. However, as an Albertan, I would also have to recognize that from the early 1950s things started to change. I would have to realize that 15, 20 or 30 years have gone by and that Albertans are perhaps the most affluent people, as a total group, in Canada. I would think my concern as an Albertan would be very much to continue this affluence and seek security. It is the insecurity that would bother me and the fact, as Mr. Hyndman would say, that oil and gas are depleting resources and as someone said over the weekend at one of the meetings in Alberta, when they are gone Albertans would become beggars. If that was on my mind, I could understand exactly why I would demand a good deal more than I was getting. I think the problem is that Mr. Hyndman tells only part of the truth. There is nothing wrong with what he is saying, but he is leaving out a very significant part.
It has been known for some time in the rest of the country and in Alberta that conventional crude oil reserves will probably be delivered by the end of the decade at about a third of the rate they are now being delivered. There is no question that the conventional crude oil resources are being depleted at a very rapid rate. There is no question that in the longer
term-perhaps in the middle or the end of the next decade- the same might happen to natural gas. I find this proposition a little harder to handle, though, because so many people in the industry are saying we have so much gas we should keep exporting it. I know the argument to the effect that the more you export, the more you discover, however, it creates a problem. But nothing is being said to the people of Alberta by their leaders-I do not think it is dishonesty; it is perhaps that it is not thought out well enough-about the long-term resources such as the tar sands, the in situ heavy oils, the coal and so on. If I were an Albertan looking at the matter as objectively as I could, I think I would conclude that Albertans will be affluent for a very, very long time; it is not something which will come and go within a decade.
1 tried to develop this theme in the House during the throne speech debate in the spring, and perhaps I am trying to say the same thing again tonight in a slightly different way. We hope the tar sands will come on. I differ strongly with the hon. member for Etobicoke Centre (Mr. Wilson) when he totally blames the tar sands holdup on this government. After all, we have offered $38 per barrel for tar sands oil and we have offered to add the inflation factor to that. We know that a year or so ago that oil could be produced at something in the order of $20 per barrel. We think that is a pretty reasonable offer for a long-term project. 1 have not heard anyone from the industry dispute that seriously, I have not heard the industry say there is anything wrong with it. Last week we lent Imperial Oil another $40 million just to keep the thing on ice, just to keep it ready to go. It seems to me that somewhere along the line the blame for this must be shared in the sense that the province of Alberta is not accepting this basically because it wants more for its other resources. So, I have difficulty in agreeing with the hon. member in this area.
If Albertans were aware of the way the deal is working out, I think they would find it quite acceptable. I tried to look through history, I tried to look at some contemporary situations in other nations, but I do not think there is any single jurisdiction in the industrial world where so much has been lavished on one group. For example, the resources in the North Sea are shared by all of Great Britain, not just the people in Aberdeen or the people in Scotland. Those most locally involved will get advantages because the activity is there, but I do not know of any place where the amount of money going to a jurisdiction is as much as is going to Alberta in this particular period. I am sure the people of Alberta are not aware of this.
The estimate-and I have not heard it questioned by anyone-is that the revenue of the Alberta government, not for production or anything like that, but just in terms of royalties and so on for oil, gas and coal, will be something in the order of $100 billion in this decade. By 1983 that will amount to $4,300 for every man, woman and child in Alberta. That will go into the Heritage Fund or whatever else is done with the royalties. If I were in the shoes of an Albertan in 1983, I would say, "It is time you distributed a little bit to us". I know that some of the Indians on the Blood Reserve have said they do
November 24, 1980

not want that money just to go into the band fund; they want it to be distributed among the people of the band. If I were in their shoes, I think I would want to do the same thing. It is a significant amount and, of course, it increases.
Today there was an argument concerning other jurisdictions in terms of their percentages. The hon. member for Annapolis Valley-Hants was totally incorrect when he said that the government of Australia owns the resources. It does not.
It does.

The Australian states only get something in the order of 20 per cent or less. It is the same in the United States of America. I do not think any other jurisdiction has ever had such an amount of money coming to it. Take a look at the other provinces in this country. This is something which is totally unique, totally new; it cannot be compared with tariffs or anything else that has ever happened to one region. I think it will last for a long time. Putting those two factors together, it seems to me that if Albertans were well aware of what was going on they would feel much more secure. I think insecurity is creating a great deal of the problem for them.
Let us look at the natural resource revenue of other provinces in 1979, the latest year for which I have figures. Newfoundland received $27 for every man, woman and child; Prince Edward Island, $3; Nova Scotia, $8; New Brunswick, $13; Quebec, $18; Ontario, $14; Manitoba, $23. Then it goes up a bit: Saskatchewan, $502; British Columbia, $221; Alberta, $1,874. We are talking about very, very large figures compared with anything else that has ever been known. We must take that uniqueness into account. I hope Albertans hear this and think about it. The things I will mention repeatedly are the amount of money, the fact that it is relatively secure and the fact that these other projects like tar sands plants which are coming along will last for a very long time.
I would like to talk about the way in which the government's policy affects the national scene and how consumers must be concerned about this. I would like to dwell on this for a minute or two since 1 come from Thunder Bay where distances are very great and where the weather is very cold. We are large users of oil, gas and whatever petroleum fuels come into our area. We have a great deal of concern about whether we can continue to function as a community in northern Ontario because of this very special problem that we face along with most Canadians to one degree or another. I do not think anyone in my area is saying we should give less to Albertans. What we are saying is that there is a national interest which must be served. We do not think it is good enough for the province of Alberta to say that they want this money so much and that they will lend it back to the CNR and the CPR. We do not think that is good enough. We think the nation must do that; national transportation priorities are something we have to deal with federally, something we cannot let a province deal with alone. There are other provinces and regions which have quite different problems.
Petroleum Administration Act
To give an illustration, there has been a lot of red-necking about the Quebecois fact and so on. I did a very rough calculation of the cost of the bilingual program in the country. In one area, it is the cost to government; in the other it is the cost of printing the other language on cornflakes boxes and so on. I calculated that the outside limit of that expenditure would be about one billion dollars a year in an economy that is in the range of $250 billion to $275 billion. That is on behalf of seven or eight million Canadians. If we take the entire amount of money that is going to Albertans per year over the decade-and it is about $10 billion-we find that is about ten times as much going to about one-quarter as many people. The factor there is about 40. I am very happy to see that we are spending the amount I mentioned on the second language. I am also pleased to see that Albertans are getting a fair share for their resources, but I must demonstrate here that we can go too far. No single jurisdiction can expect much more than is being given at this time.
I will conclude now as my time is just about up. I will return to my initial idea and say that my party, which has formed the government for most of this century, basically because we have been a middle-of-the-road party and have not gone to extremes one way or the other-
Look at the west!

I left your party to come over here for one reason, which is simply that I did not think this country could be put together by extremes. One of the reasons the Progressive Conservative Party is not in power right now is because they got off that mainstream. What this party has done over the years is stay in that mainstream.
The muddled middle.
I believe the policy we are adopting at this moment with respect to the amount of money in that package is fair and reasonable and in the long term it will be recognized as such in this country.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) is rising on a point of order?
If he still has time, I wonder if the hon. member would permit a question.
Mr. Speaker, I think I have a minute left.

The hon. member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan (Mr. McRae) seemed to indicate he did not trust the provinces with respect to his point about offshore resources. Specifically, he did not trust the province of Newfoundland to protect those resources from multinational companies. Looking at the record of the other provinces like British Columbia, Saskatchewan and Quebec, would he not agree that they have a better record of taking control of resources than the Government of Canada which has allowed our energy resources, our oil and gas, to be 82 per cent foreign-controlled? Where does he obtain the evidence for his argument that compared to the Government of

November 24, 1980
Petroleum Administration Act
Canada the provinces are weak-kneed when it comes to dealing with multinationals?

I believe what I said is true. Certain jurisdictions which are very progressive, have probably done a better job, in particular the province of Quebec, in relation to the asbestos company. I remember attending mass in the church at Dorval and listening to the Archbishop speaking about the strike at the asbestos plant. It was a very thrilling moment for me. In the province of Quebec these resources were controlled by multinational corporations for a long time. In my view, the multinationals think a smaller jurisdiction is easier to handle. The production costs have been assessed in the Islands. The data available suggest that the fuel savings make the use of wind energy probably the most economical solution, since it is less expensive to produce one kilowatt hour by this method than to produce the same amount of electricity with oil. The data have hardly been collected and they are already thinking about increasing the output through larger facilities. It is planned, for example, to set up in Quebec in 1983 an $18 million machine capable of supplying electricity to 600 or 700 households. We all know that the sky is the limit in this area. It is to be hoped that governments, through budgetary incentives for instance, will give high priority to ongoing projects and to the building of new facilities so as to promote the tapping of wind-generated energy.
Mr. Speaker, when speaking a moment ago about the producing provinces, I touched upon the matter of federal-provincial relations within the context of the national energy policy. I already said as well that consultation was an essential condition to the implementation of this program. But what is true for Alberta is also true for Quebec.
As concerns the province of Quebec in particular, priorities in energy matters for the next ten years have been clearly defined in the premier's inaugural speech. Essentially, Quebec is planning to invest about $55 billion in the Quebec Hydro development program, especially in the harnessing of secondary rivers. Then, the province will launch an operation to replace oil as an energy source through the development of natural gas. In that last instance, the federal contribution and that of the producing provinces will have to be planned so as to allow true consultation. That is why our government has already approved the extension of a natural gas pipeline from Montreal to Quebec City. In addition, it is hoped that the gas pipeline will be extended to the maritimes, so as to cover the eastern part of Quebec. Also, discussions are proceeding on the route of the natural gas pipeline.
Then, Quebec should place itself above political bickering for the well-being of all its citizens. Until now, the minister of energy for Quebec has expressed some reservation about the program to convert from oil to other energy sources. However, he opened the door to a greater co-ordination of programs particularly the one aimed at promoting the use of natural gas. However, as it goes with any major project, it must be well understood that time will be the determining factor in order for public funds to be used for the well-being, the security and the availability of natural resources for the benefit of each Canadian consumer. And as was observed recently by our
November 24, 1980

colleague and Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, it is a tremendous and difficult challenge.
Mr. Speaker, the big difference between the world of scientists and the world of consumers is assuredly their concept of the future. As far as they are concerned, governments should get involved in both these areas. And especially since World War II, the role of the government has greatly expanded to such an extent that there has been a renewal of the schools of thought in favour of economic liberalism.
Today, people have clearly expressed their desire to see governments let go of their hold on the individual. However, it will be noted that the wind did not blow as hard as expected by the previous government who tried to initiate a so-called energy policy. Its policy was based, indeed, on an overbearing will which paid little attention to the taxpayers: the dismantling of Petro-Canada, accelerated increases in oil prices, etc.
Mr. Speaker, from this statement it appears that the government's intentions cannot escape from the international realities. As in many other industrialized countries, Canadians have had to learn to live with inflation. This means, among other things, that we accept, whether we like it or not, doing business using a currency which fluctuates according to the circumstances. This also means that we will have to put up with the inconvenience of skyrocketing prices. In other words, we pay more to get less. Concepts like the scarcity of goods and the net loss of buying power will have resulted in the weakening of what was called the American way of life. But at some time or other Canadians experienced periods when it was difficult to obtain the bare necessities.
The rationing system implemented during World War II is one of the factors which restricted our freedom to consume. But seldom will Canadians be as concerned with regard to their future as have been industrialized countries as a whole. Mass consumption is about to yield to a new way of life or, even better, to a modus vivendi which will require a greater choice and a better selection to meet our aspirations and our needs. It has almost become unsafe to speak of economic recovery as a direct result of successive events at the international level.
Recently, OECD reports suggested careful optimism for the years to come. Unemployment rates will reach unprecedented levels affecting about 20 million people of all ages and all walks of life. More recently, the United Nations warned us about the food supplies of some countries: The outlook for world supplies and the security of food in 1981 is so bad that there is an over-all emergency situation. It points to the situation in Africa, for example, as being quite alarming in view of the fact that grain imports in 1979-1980 increased by 21 million tons or 19 per cent over the preceding season. On top of this there was a deterioration of the political climate in several areas of the world.
Petroleum Administration Act
Mr. Speaker, we cannot possibly think that some miraculous system could remedy all these problems. For several years we praised the merits of so-called planned economies but even those have felt the ill-effects of the oil crisis. Leaders of communist countries, for example, quickly realized that their production of goods and services fell behind the levels anticipated or planned for the short or long term. That is why, as the Economic Council of Canada noted in its fourth annual report, objectives will have to be balanced if we want to achieve sustained economic growth. The key to success, therefore, lies in the choices to be made and must be aimed at the well-being of all Canadians. Future efforts toward a greater use of renewable energy present a major challenge which will be beneficial to this and future generations. Mr. Speaker, now is the time to act. The government, with this national energy policy, calls upon all Canadians to participate asking them to act sensibly and with good spirit in the use of our country's energy potential.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to refer to an article which appeared in the November 22 edition of the Financial Post. It reads as follows:
The New York investment banker who floats multibillion-dollar issues for a gaggle of Canadian governments (and for that reason, who chooses anonymity) is puzzled.
"I can't get this straight," he says over the phone. "Your government says it wants self-sufficiency in oil. It wants to encourage Canadian companies. So it brings in a policy that results in Canadian companies coming down here to help the U.S., while the U.S. subsidiaries left up there cut back their Canadian exploration budgets. Does this make sense to you?"
No, Mr. Speaker. Sections 35 and 36 of the Petroleum Administration Act allow the government to unilaterally impose prices if no agreement is reached with the producing provinces. It begs the question: why was the government unable to reach an agreement with Alberta?
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) would have us believe that he walked miles and miles to reach an agreement. That is a total sham, it was a show staged for the media and for the public. He made lots of mileage out of it, but he did not even come close to an agreement, nor would it appear that he had any intention of doing so.
The minister of energy for Alberta outlined the meetings he had with the federal Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. May 13 was a "get-together" meeting; they had coffee, they discussed the weather. On June 18 one proposal was discussed, the one which is essentially in the energy package today. When it was not accepted by the Alberta government on June 18, the minister asked the provincial energy minister to remain until June 19. He said he would take it back to his colleagues. The indications were that he came back on June 19, at which time he offered an absolutely ridiculous proposal which was worse than the first, knowing full well that it would not be approved. It would appear he
5022	_______COMMONS
Petroleum Administration Act
wanted to keep up the appearance of negotiations, so that people would think they were still negotiating.
After meeting with Mr. Lougheed in July, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) stated that Alberta had made a very generous offer to the rest of Canada, but he announced that there was no agreement. I suggest that the government never intended to reach an agreement with Alberta, that it had set the goal of nationalization of the oil industry, that it was prepared to go full steam ahead, and damn the consequences. The government is prepared to challenge any provincial government for jurisdiction unilaterally if that province appears to be breaking its economic dependence on the central government. It is the aim of the present government to remain in power at all cost, and, of course, that is "by Goldfarb". If this were not the case, we would not be debating the imposition of sections 35 and 36 of the Petroleum Administration Act. Such an act should only be used when all else fails. Every possible avenue must be explored before these sections are imposed. They should never be used to club a provincial government into submission. What will the imposition of these sections of the act do? First, it will provide cannon shells to an increasingly militant group in western Canada, particularly in Alberta. If I mention this only briefly, it is not because it is unimportant. Responsible men and women are saying, "Let's get out of this mess." Nothing is more dangerous to our country today than the attitude which is starting to fester in western Canada.
The minister would have us believe that the imposition of this act may be rescinded at any time, if an agreement is reached with the provinces. I refer you, Mr. Speaker, to the debates of November 21 and I would like to quote from page 4964 of Hansard for that date in which the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources is reported as saying:
-we indicated that as soon as an agreement could be reached, we would be willing and ready to rescind those proclamations in order to work on the basis of an agreement.
I also refer you to page 4967 of the same date on which the minister said:
It was to ensure a certain degree of certainty and clarification as to the government's policy that it was decided to put forward this long-term plan. We have indicated that this is a ten-year program.
Further down the page he says:
We have put forward a pricing regime which we think will be fair for the industry over the next ten years and for the various regions of the country.
I suggest that if the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources is ready to enter into negotiations with the province of Alberta those statements are contradictory. In no way has he created a climate for proper negotiations. I do not suspect for one moment that the government is willing or ready to change its position on the energy policy budget brought down on black Tuesday. I suggest it will continue in exactly the way it is going-no negotiation whatsoever that will bear fruit. What has happened? No agreement and no oil sands plants.
Let me focus on the oil sands and tar sands. I know there has been a lot of fall-out because of the energy program, the
DEBATES	November 24, 1980
budget and no agreement. Let me focus on those factors. There is Cold Lake, which is the Imperial Oil project worth $8 billion. There is private capital waiting to be invested in northeastern Alberta for the benefit of all Canada. There is Alsands in Fort McMurray, another $8 billion of private capital ready to be invested in northeastern Alberta for the benefit of all Canada.
What is the benefit of one plant? Let us deal with them one at a time, looking at Alsands first. Alsands will produce 137,000 to 140,000 barrels per day. It can start up production in 1988. It was to be 1987 but it has now been delayed one year. It will operate like a factory for a term of 25 years producing 140,000 barrels per day every day. The total capital investment will be $8 billion to $9 billion, creating 8,000 jobs during construction. Over 80 per cent of the material and equipment will be purchased in Canada. This will reduce oil imports and will improve the balance of payments by $40 billion over the life of the project. That figure is in 1980 dollars. The economic benefits to Canada as a whole have been estimated at $100 billion. That, too, is in 1980 dollars. The benefit to Alberta will amount to $66 billion. Ontario, as a centre of Canadian manufacturing, will benefit from secure oil supply and increased demand for equipment and materials, both during construction and operation. Of course, it will reduce unemployment.
What are some of the requirements? They are: major equipment; columns and vessels, $109 million; tanks, $31 million; exchangers, $73 million; fired heaters, $70 million; pumps and drivers, $44 million; compressors and drivers, $41 million; extraction equipment, $109 million; mining and material handling equipment, $496 million; boilers and steam turbines, $31 million; instruments, $67 million; piping, $233 million; structural steel, $52 million; insulation, $29 million; electrical, $173 million. The list goes on and on.
Who will benefit from the purchase of this equipment? Central Canada. It is the lifeblood of the manufacturing industry. It creates jobs.
Look at the Esso project at Cold Lake which commenced in 1963, 17 years ago, at a total construction cost of $9 billion. We hear consistently from our NDP friends: Let Petro-Canada do it. Questioned in the Standing Committee on Natural Resources, Petro-Canada indicated it would be ten years before they would be ready to proceed even with the first stages of a heavy oil or tar sands plant. The Esso project is the first of its kind anywhere in the world. It is a joint research project. The private venture capital of $8 billion, Mr. Speaker, is waiting to be invested to prove technology. On completion the plant will produce 140,000 barrels per day. It will contribute $2 billion plus a year to our balance of payments. Again, this project has a life of 25 years. The total crude to be produced is expected to be 1.3 billion barrels. In its peak construction period it will employ 10,000 people. The plant will employ 2,000 to 3,000 people when it is built. Indirectly, it will produce jobs for 6,500 people. It does not stop there. The Esso Cold Lake plant will cost $9 billion to construct. Related facilities will cost another $1 billion. The infrastructure will
November 24, 1980

cost another $1 billion. The investment on a continuing basis will be $20 billion. Operating expenses over 25 years will be $60 billion. That represents a total expenditure of $90 billion with a normal multiplier of $250 billion to $300 billion in the economy of Canada.
The stupidity and vindictiveness of this government never ceases to amaze me. Our entire energy future is being jeopardized by confrontation politics, all because the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde), with a preconceived idea, will not sit down and negotiate in good faith with the province of Alberta. Ted Byfield said in the Alberta report of November 7, 1980, that this was a calamitous year. The article took me back to last November and the time when the final touches were being put on an oil agreement between the then Conservative government of Canada and the government of the province of Alberta.
Had that agreement been allowed to stand, he said, consider what the situation would have been today. The Cold Lake and Alsands plants would have gone forward at full throttle, exploration would have been proceeding on the whole northern and eastern rim of this continent, the pipeline construction would have been under way as would the exploration of the further reaches of the deep basin which holds such promise. Mr. Byfield felt that oil rig operators would have been desperate for men. Investment capital reaching across the whole west would have been opening new jobs and new opportunities. Billions of dollars in equipment orders would have been streaming forth to central Canadian plants and our provinces would have been working hand in hand with the federal government toward a goal which everyone would have clearly understood, oil self-sufficiency by 1990. All that could have been.
I submit that the most important factor to be considered in Canada today is an insecure energy supply and, therefore, the necessity of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources to meet with his counterpart in Alberta to hammer out an agreement. The government is jeopardizing the future of all Canada by failing to sit down and work out that agreement.
I would like to present a few points for the government to consider. Canada is a net importer of costly, insecure oil- about 350,000 barrels a day. These imports contribute to an adverse balance of payments. Conventional reserves are declining rapidly. Canada has reserves of hydrocarbons in the tar sands and heavy oil deposits to last for centuries. It is a known and reliable resource and the technology is available to develop it. There is some risk involved but the technology is there.
Current costs for a major tar sands project of 140,000 barrels a day would amount to about $8 billion or $9 billion. What is the problem? Why is the government not developing this vast resource? There is an absence of a dependable ongoing policy on pricing, royalties and taxation to give industry the confidence required to proceed with the development of the resource; I need only refer hon. members to the Suncor problem.
Petroleum Administration Act
What does the future offer? The balance of payments position will worsen as imports are increased. Imports in 1978 cost Canada $1.8 billion. On the basis of a price estimate at $240 a barrel by the year 2000, we could still be importing 500,000 barrels of oil per day at a cost of $44 billion per year. That is staggering. The security of our supply situation is not likely to improve. We must develop an acceptable policy on pricing, royalties and taxation and a realistic, well-planned program for optimum utilization of all Canada's energy resources. Such a program would provide an opportunity to turn the economy around by reducing imports and even to begin exporting in the future.
In order to provide materials and services for these huge megaprojects, the government should develop programs to gear up all of Canada. It must recreate an atmosphere of co-operation rather than confrontation. The technology and equipment of the tar sands and heavy oil industry could be exported to other parts of the world. Oil companies do not want to get involved in politics, but rather, want all levels of government to provide a good business climate in which to operate.
To Canadianize the industry would require a long-term, realistic plan to cope with the ownership problem. It would require a reasonable rate of return higher than the accepted utility rate of return because the risk is greater. There are many advantages to such a program. There would be self-sufficiency and security of supply so we could all sleep at night. It would reduce our adverse balance of payments position and strengthen the Canadian dollar; it would improve the over-all economic situation of Canada. We could possibly find ourselves in a position to export oil if such steps were taken. These proposals would create many employment opportunities for our children and their grandchildren. No longer would they be leaving university, trade schools and colleges not knowing whether they will have a job or not; our economy will be healthy and able to absorb these graduates.
Mr. Speaker, we are on the verge of creating a technological expertise which, one day, will be needed all over the world. The technology we have gained in the heavy oil and tar sands industry is saleable to other countries. We could help to create a more unified Canada and believe me, Mr. Speaker, that is the main objective. Thank you.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take part in this debate tonight, in the few minutes that are left, to speak of the proclamation under the Petroleum Administration Act, which opposition members ask to be revoked because in their view the federal government should not unilaterally have set prices. I can understand that members of the Progressive Conservative Party should take that position but I have difficulty understanding why the New Democrats say that we should not have acted unilaterally when, after six months of fruitless discussions the two parties

Petroleum Administration Act
have been unable to reach an agreement. I find that strange coming from a party which has always said that the federal government should have greater control over the economy since, according to the basic philosophy of the CCF, that was the way to achieve socialism in Canada.
If it is opposed to the federal government's unilateral move in setting prices, the NDP should at least not try to make believe that it does so out of respect for Alberta's and B.C.'s position. It wants to play both sides at once and still be loyal and faithful to the position it took in the past and in recent years, since it would probably have imposed a much more rigid price than the one set by the present government.
Mr. Speaker, when we hear people say that the federal government has been too harsh on Alberta, we should consider a few facts. First, for about five years the federal government's share of oil revenues was about 10 per cent, whereas the producing provinces' share was a little more than 45 per cent and the industry's a little less than 45 per cent. In his budget of October 28, the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) proposed some changes. Instead of being shared 45, 45, 10, revenues would be split 43 per cent for producing provinces, 33 per cent for industry and about 24 per cent for the federal government. In other words, the budget reduced by only 2 per cent the producing provinces' share, while increasing the federal government's share by 14 per cent to 24 per cent. It is therefore not Alberta, British Columbia or Saskatchewan which lose a great deal, but industry. The industry's share goes from 45 per cent down to 33 per cent. It is quite strange to see the NDP oppose such a change. On the other hand it is easy to understand that the Tories should be against it, as they have always claimed that it was bad for government, whether federal or provincial, to get too involved in the nation's business.
Let us consider whether the federal government's position is really ungenerous. During the coming four years, Alberta would receive $31 billion from the oil industry, Saskatchewan $3.2 billion and British Columbia $3.6 billion. Mr. Speaker, the situation is quite simple. We have to ask ourselves now whether our central government will be looking after the interests of all Canadians. Such is the question that has to be asked, because we know that energy is the most important asset for the future development of our society.
We will have to invest in Canada over $250 billion for energy purposes during the next ten years. This means that from now on our economy will be energy oriented. If we want a government that looks after the interests of all Canadians, how will such a government wield the necessary power if it has no money? How will a government which is supposed to look after the interests of all Canadians be able to do so, that is, conduct future energy development, protect the poor after steep price increases, give areas of the country deprived of natural gas and oil other forms of energy and bring together
November 24, 1980
the productive regions of the country and those which do not have any.
But how can it be done unless the federal treasury has money in its coffers? I would like people and the Progressive Conservative Party to explain to me how they would have the federal government take care of Canadian interests without money. To hear them, they would like Alberta and the producing provinces to continue receiving an important share, as well as the others. For our part, we want to leave them 43 per cent. What is it they do not like? Is it the fact that the share of the industry will be reduced from 45 per cent to 33 per cent? Are they willing to allow the companies to develop and operate freely, as they see fit, simply by reaching agreements with the producing provinces?
Mr. Speaker, I doubt that it can be done. Eater on in my speech which I shall bring to an end tomorrow, I shall explain why it is important, even outside the energy question, to protect the federal treasury. I had an analysis made of the difference between the expenditures of the federal government in the last five years and those incurred by the provincial governments. I also had one made of the percentage of the federal budget that is used to finance the debt compared to those of the provinces. And I shall demonstrate, later on in my speech, how close we are getting to having a federal government which, compared with its provincial counterparts, will be unable to look after the interests of all Canadians. Who will then take care of those interests? The ten provincial governments in a common effort? A community of communities? How amusing to remember how the Deader of the Progressive Conservative Party, who was prime minister for nine months, started in that office saying that we are a community of communities. But just before the last election, he had to admit in a speech given in Alberta that he understood why it is important to maintain a strong central government, which means that in the fields of energy and taxes, the federal government should have a greater share of the revenues.
So, that was sheer hypocrisy on the part of the Conservatives to change their minds today, now that they are in the opposition and want to make political hay out of the fact that some people out west are not happy with the government's energy policy and to say that the government is hogging it. Their leader realized, Mr. Speaker, when he was prime minister, even if it was for only nine months, that it is important to have a federal government with full coffers and not just debts.
I see it is ten o'clock, Mr. Speaker. I shall continue tomorrow.
November 24, 1980
A motion to adjourn the House under Standing Order 40 deemed to have been moved.

subtopic: ENERGY-REPORTED ESTABLISHMENT OF WESTERN ENERGY DEVELOPMENT FUND
ENERGY-REPORTED ESTABLISHMENT OF WESTERN ENERGY DEVELOPMENT FUND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on October 16 as recorded at page 3720 of Hansard 1 addressed specific questions to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) relating to speculation that the government's budget would contain reference to something called the western development fund and a natural gas export tax.
In fact, it was the leader of the government in the Senate who announced in mid-September that such a development fund would indeed be part of the budget, only to have that announcement denied by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) a few days later. I felt at the time that my questions were pertinent. The second question which dealt with the natural gas export tax has also proven to be most pertinent. In fact, over 32,000 residents in British Columbia in the four-week period between the middle of September and the middle of October signed petitions opposing the implementation of any form of federal tax on the natural gas resources of British Columbia which would be exported from that province.
The reason I asked the two questions of these ministers was to determine the extent to which the Liberal party was prepared to honour its commitment made clearly and unequivocally to the people of British Columbia during the last election campaign. During that campaign they stated there would not be any form of natural gas tax levied on the export of natural gas; there was a suggestion, at least, that the federal government did not have its eyes on provincial resources for the purpose of raising federal revenues, a suggestion which has proven to be completely untrue. We have seen with the passage of the October 28 budget that both the natural gas export tax and the western development fund have come to pass. I suppose we ought to be grateful for the token western development fund which was thrown into the budget-I might say it was a $2 million slap in the face to British Columbians, because in the period during which that western development fund would return $2 billion in resource revenues to the western provinces, this same federal government will expropriate over $14 billion worth of revenue which it will raise by levying various forms of taxation against the production of those natural resources which, to this date, belong to the western provinces. If the western provinces have their way, these natural resources will belong to those provinces for a long time to come.
The budget includes a petroleum compensation charge, a natural gas tax and an 8 per cent federal tax on net revenues
Adjournment Debate
from the production of gas and oil as well as a Canadian ownership tax. This myriad of taxes so craftily and sneakily incorporated into the budget add up to a tax levy on the people of western Canada amounting to at least $14 billion between now and the end of 1984, in other words, over the next three fiscal years.
The thrust of my question to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources was to determine whether he had any conscience about promising that the government would give back a pitiful $2 billion while craftily extracting $14 billion out of the pockets of western Canadian producers, provincial treasuries and indeed the consumers of western Canada, Ontario, and Quebec, all of whom will be hit hard by these unconscionable taxes which the federal government is imposing. The natural gas tax will have a significant impact on British Columbia where revenues totalled $320 million to the provincial treasury in the last fiscal year through the medium of the British Columbia Petroleum Corporation.
The federal government, under the proposals of the present budget, will expropriate or take $200 million of this revenue each year when we reach the schedule of 60 cents per thousand cubic feet levied, as well as the 8 per cent federal tax on natural gas. This amounts to $200 million per year taken out of British Columbia to contribute to this so-called concept of sharing, which 1 will come to in a moment. That $200 million will be distributed between all consumers of natural gas in British Columbia, not only industry but home owners who heat their homes with natural gas. Another $100 million will be taken from the producers, but ultimately from the treasury of British Columbia, in lieu of exports of natural gas from B.C. which will be subject to this tax. The consequence to the consumer is a $40 increase in the home heating bill this winter and a doubling of the surcharge next year. That will place an unfair and undue discriminatory burden upon the people of my province and those in western Canada generally.
I want to say a word about the concept of sharing. We in the western part of this country are sick and tired of the Liberal myth which suggests that somehow we are selfish. That is absolutely untrue. It is a political myth which the party opposite perpetuates most dishonestly. The western concept of sharing is that we want to share our resources, and sharing is an outward gesture which involves generosity and mutual consent. That is quite contrary to the Trudeau concept of sharing, which amounts to unilateral confiscation of western resources, the resources of the people of the provinces as granted to them under the British North America Act.
The federal government will not account for the net costs to some of the provinces of the confiscation of those resources. It is atrocious that government members can sit in their places and show no sense of conscience about this issue or the right of resource ownership to which all provinces have been entitled since the time they joined confederation.

speakeroldname: Mr. Roy MacLaren (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: ENERGY-REPORTED ESTABLISHMENT OF WESTERN ENERGY DEVELOPMENT FUND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in response to

November 24, 1980
Adjournment Debate
the hon. member's comments, I could spend a moment or two on the question of the application of various taxes he has cited. He seemed to think they had a regional impact of a grossly disproportionate character. If he wanted, for example, to take the case he cited of the natural gas tax, he would find that the major burden of that tax would fall on the people of Ontario. About 44 per cent of the revenue from the application of that tax will be raised in Ontario.
However, in the few moments I have available, 1 think it would be better to address ourselves to some more positive elements and to note that, along with a variety of other new energy expenditures and initiatives, the national energy program announced the establishment of the western development fund. This special ten-year, $4 billion fund has been set up to finance a series of economic development initiatives to be chosen jointly by both the federal government and the individual governments of the four western provinces.
The federal government will not make any unilateral decisions relative to the disposition of these funds. The western provinces will be genuine partners in any decision to be made on where and how allotted funds will be spent.
While 1 do not propose to make judgments on where this money will be spent, I would anticipate that much of this funding will be used for infrastructure improvements in the west, especially in transport, for industrial development and diversification, for agricultural programs and for water resource development which will be required for the tar sands and hydro projects.
The Government of Canada will also examine, as a matter of priority, how its trade policies could be strengthened or modified to encourage diversified growth of western Canada's economy.
The federal government is most interested in assisting western Canada in diversifying its economic base which has been traditionally dependent on non-renewable resources. The national energy program has outlined the government's desire not to see more oil-based petrochemical capacity in eastern Canada. This means that the concentration of future growth within this industry will take place in western Canada, notably in Alberta. The federal government promises to support fully this trend of western diversification.
The benefits to be derived from the western development fund are additional to the many other benefits which will result from other initiatives of the national energy program. The pricing regime, particularly as it is designed to encourage the development of the oil sands and the heavy oil areas, will lead to major opening up of these resources and, as a spin-off, the growth of many new supply and service industries. The new initiatives system for oil and gas exploration will lead to broadening the resource base and the industries that are allied to resource development activity. Such programs as financial support for a gas pipeline to Vancouver Island, the construction of a heavy oil upgrader in Saskatchewan and a number of conservation and renewable energy programs in Manitoba will
all assist in the resource development and industrial diversification process.

subtopic: CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY-WINNIPEG-INQUIRY WHETHER PERMIT TO BUILD OVERPASS WILL BE AUTHORIZED
CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY-WINNIPEG-INQUIRY WHETHER PERMIT TO BUILD OVERPASS WILL BE AUTHORIZED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am rising tonight to speak about the issuing of the CTC permit for the building of the Sherbrook-McGregor overpass, and I hope this is the last time I will have to bring this issue up in the House of Commons because there has been an undue delay over the last couple of years with regard to the issuing of this permit.
1 received an assurance last week from the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) and the chairman of the Canadian Transport Commission that the permit will be issued to the city of Winnipeg to go ahead, finally, with the building of the Sherbrook-McGregor overpass, which should have been built in the first place. I will go into that in a little more detail in a moment.
I see the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Bockstael) here tonight. He is the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport, and I hope he will confirm that the permit will be issued this week.

subtopic: CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY-WINNIPEG-INQUIRY WHETHER PERMIT TO BUILD OVERPASS WILL BE AUTHORIZED
speechtext:
My main reason for raising this issue tonight is the cost overrun which the city of Winnipeg has had to suffer because of the ridiculous nonsense we have had to put up with over the last almost two years with regard to the issuing of this permit.
The original delay and stoppage of the permit was caused by the present Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy), the hon. member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry, who used his authority as a Liberal to have the permit withheld. He talked a former minister of transport, Mr. Otto Lang, into stopping the issuing of the permit to build the overpass, stating that there should be rail relocation. Nobody is opposed to rail relocation, but the first thing he should have done was check federal Liberal policy to find out whether there were funds available for rail relocation and whether there was a firm policy for going ahead with rail relocation. If he had checked that first, he would have found that the government had dropped its policy of funding rail relocation. He might then
November 24, 1980

have stopped his pilgrimage to pursue this rail relocation issue in Winnipeg.
Instead of checking first, the Minister of Employment and Immigration had the permit stopped. This has caused the city of Winnipeg no end of problems, and there is a cost overrun of some $2.5 million.
I am on my feet tonight hoping that the hon. member for St. Boniface will let us know what he is going to do about getting this $2.5 million for the city of Winnipeg. As a former councillor the hon. member is well aware of the Sherbrook-McGregor overpass and all of the implications. He has an obligation to the city of Winnipeg to see that the city is reimbursed that $2.5 million, the cost of the overrun, because of the interference of the Minister of Employment and Immigration.
February 20, 1979, was the date on which the Minister of Employment and Immigration called for a delay in the construction of the overpass, and this interruption has cost the city of Winnipeg about $2.5 million. That figure is based upon a cost of $7,000 per day for delays in the construction of the overpass.
I should like to go into some of the history in connection with this sham and the confusion caused by the unnecessary interference of the Minister of Employment and Immigration. In June, 1980, the Minister of Transport authorized the construction of the Sherbrook-McGregor overpass which ended a 14-month delay and forced the cost to rise by $2 million to $20 million. Of course, as of today it is $2.5 million. Mayor Bill Norrie stated that he would begin the battle to get Ottawa to cover the increased costs, and I am continuing the battle here tonight. We will keep after the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport to do something about this issue. There is no use going after the Minister of Employment and Immigration; it would be an absolute waste of time.
The project was delayed by the federal government pending a study on the cost of rail relocation. On that basis Mayor Norrie said that he felt the city had a good case for increased federal aid. The city and the province of Manitoba did not ask for this rail study. If there were a firm commitment from the federal government in respect of rail relocation-they had about $1 billion in funds set aside because other cities would also want rail relocation-then the city and the province would have been required to come up with money for rail relocation and there would have been justification for it. Everybody except the Minister of Employment and Immigration knew that the federal government did not have the money or had no intention of putting up the money. The President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) made it perfectly clear that there were no funds for rail relocation. So the cost overruns are the direct responsibility of the present Liberal government.
I want a statement from the parliamentary secretary tonight confirming that the permit is being issued, and also, as a member of Parliament from Manitoba he should let us know
Adjournment Debate
what he will do about recovering this $2.5 million for the city of Winnipeg. This nonsense has gone on long enough. The parliamentary secretary made some statements in the past indicating that the minister will not provide the funding and that he will not do anything about it. That is not good enough for me or for the citizens of Winnipeg. The parliamentary secretary has an obligation to speak up and indicate what he intends to do about getting the $2.5 million for the city of Winnipeg.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY-WINNIPEG-INQUIRY WHETHER PERMIT TO BUILD OVERPASS WILL BE AUTHORIZED

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member's original question on June 2 was sparked by the announcement that there would be a core area initiative for the city of Winnipeg. The initiative consisted of a five-year program under which federal funds would be provided to enable the city to respond to various social and economic problems in the downtown area.
At the time of the announcement, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) indicated that it was up to the city and the province to decide the course of action they wish to follow with respect to the Sherbrook-McGregor grade separation. He said that if the consensus was to build an overpass, he was prepared to approve funding for construction immediately under the Urban Transportation Assistance Program. Previously the province indicated that it was prepared to dedicate $7.6 million of its UTAP allotment for this purpose. The city and the province confirmed their desire for an overpass, and on June 16 the minister approved the $7.6 million UTAP contribution. I mention the date to emphasize how fast the federal response was once the final position of the city and the province had been received.
Normally, the Canadian Transport Commission would have issued a construction order shortly thereafter to allow construction to begin. However, Rossbrook House, a community organization which opposed the overpass, took various steps to attempt to block its construction. It applied to the CTC asking that the construction not be permitted on the basis that a safety hazard would exist. Rossbrook House also appealed to the Federal Court asking that the federal contribution be quashed on a technicality. The application to the CTC has just recently been denied. Though the court appeal has not yet been settled the CTC feels it cannot hold back the project because of this and intends to issue a construction order in a matter of days. I understand the city plans to start the actual work in the spring.
The delay in getting this needed project under way is regrettable but I am sure the hon. member will understand the reason I have just outlined. The overpass, along with the funds provided under the broader core area initiative, will go a long way toward improving conditions in downtown Winnipeg. As such, the federal initiative has been welcomed by both the city and the province.

subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE-STATUS OF WOMEN-EQUAL PAY FOR WORK OF EQUAL VALUE
PUBLIC SERVICE-STATUS OF WOMEN-EQUAL PAY FOR WORK OF EQUAL VALUE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on a number of occasions in the last six months I have raised issues in this Elouse questioning the Liberal government's commitment to achieving equality in the workplace. I am talking about equality for groups which have been disenfranchised or which have been receiving unequal treatment in the past-women's groups, native groups, the physically handicapped and others.
I have a number of reasons for believing that the government has no real commitment in this area. We have questioned them in the past on paid maternity leave. We have questioned them in the past on affirmative action programs. We have questioned them on whether or not they are really committed to equal pay for work of equal or comparable value. This is a problem which is not faced in the government sector alone; it is faced in all sectors of the Canadian economy. In all cases the Liberal government has been afraid to act. I think the reason for this fear is their own slow progress when it comes to affirmative action programs.
In 1972 there was a cabinet directive encouraging managers to hire women. Yet eight years later we find the women in the public service overlooked and underpaid. In a document prepared by the National Advisory Committee on the Status of Women it is pointed out that it will take 66 years at the present pace to achieve any equality. In other words, it will take until the year 2046 A.D. before we have equality in the public service, at the rate the government is proceeding at this time. In that document they pointed out that 60 per cent of women are still working as clerks and secretaries. They point out that in only three of 100 government departments and agencies are there any affirmative action programs at all. Most senior executive positions are still occupied by men and there has not been much change at the level of the younger executives. In the senior executive group, of 200 under 40 years of age only 16 are women. When we turn to the senior executives under the age of 35 we find only three out of 34 are women.
In all these areas we find that the pace has been very slow. The government has not acted. Instead, the government has reacted. It has not been initiating programs, instead it has been reacting to human rights cases brought against it. It has taken a long time to act even in those cases. First of all, the union applies to the Human Rights Commission. The Human Rights Commission invariably responds by saying that the government has acted wrongly. Then there is a slow follow-up by Treasury Board before it acts in this area. So people who have been suffering from unequal treatment by government for years and years find that it takes years and years more to get action by the government after that.
What our party has been saying is that instead of taking this passive approach the government should take a positive
approach. This was suggested by my leader in a letter he wrote to the minister in June. He asked for an approach by which the government is committed into looking into each and every one of its departments and agencies to make sure action is taken affirmatively.
Last week I called for a comparative wage study, a co-operative wage study in which both union and management would sit down and draw up job descriptions to ensure that people in the public service are being paid for what they are doing, not on the basis of whether they are male or female. I am sure that whichever parliamentary secretary has been deemed the expert for tonight will talk about the great progress, the new initiatives and the recent actions of the government. I suspect that some parliamentary secretary said exactly the same thing, back in 1972, "We have written a directive encouraging management to act", and so on. But nothing has happened. 1 hope that the parliamentary secretary will not give the usual blase answer tonight but will say instead that the government is committed to doing something on the matter. I will give him a chance now.

speakeroldname: Mr. Doug Frith (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Deputy Leader of the Government in the Senate
subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE-STATUS OF WOMEN-EQUAL PAY FOR WORK OF EQUAL VALUE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hope I do not disappoint the hon. member. The question he has raised this evening has attracted the close interest of the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) as he is most concerned with the expeditious implementation of the Canadian Human Rights Act.
As hon. members may be aware, Mr. Speaker, section 11 of the act introduced a new concept, adopted by very few jurisdictions around the world, one without any appreciable jurisprudence elsewhere. Under the equal pay for work of equal value concept, in contrast to the normal provision of equal pay for the same or like work, jobs of quite different nature may be compared, using job evaluation techniques to determine whether they have the same intrinsic value. This is a new and untried approach to the elimination of pay discrimination.
Prior to the 1978 proclamation of the Canadian Human Rights Act, the Treasury Board submitted a brief on the equal pay concept to the Canadian Human Rights Commission. Subsequently, ongoing meetings have been held with officials of the commission in attempts to clarify the application of the new concept to the complex area of collective bargaining and compensation administration.
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to report that over a year ago, in anticipation of the need, a universal job evaluation plan, the Aiken Plan, was adapted from the private sector for use in resolution of equal pay complaints. This plan has been accepted by the commission as being free of sex bias and is being used in current pay discrimination complaints.
To date, the Canadian Human Rights Commission has notified the employer of six complaints accepted for investigation. The first three were related to nurses in penitentiaries and have been settled on terms agreeable to the employer, the commission and the original complainants. The fourth case
November 24, 1980

involved a director of nursing versus other directors in a hospital. This complaint was settled on November 17 of this year and is in the process of implementation.
With respect to the case from Churchill raised by the hon. member, that of the general services group, the secretary of the Treasury Board informed the Canadian Human Rights Commission on May 20 of the employer's agreement that a case of sex discrimination affecting pay, within the terms of the legislation, exists. The commission, Treasury Board Canada and the Public Service Alliance of Canada have held discussions on possible settlement alternatives, and a settlement proposal is in preparation. Officials of Treasury Board have been instructed to tackle the problems of applying the
Adjournment Debate
principle of equal pay for work of equal value to this group of employees as expeditiously as possible.
In addition to the foregoing and in order to allow the employer to take the initiative rather than merely responding to complaints, a study in depth has been authorized to commence in the new year with the object of identifying and removing pay discrimination in the public service.
